title: CrashActivity is posted to the main looper inside the uncaught-exception handler, so it (almost) never actually launches
detail: The uncaught handler does Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).post { CrashActivity.start(...) } and then immediately delegates to previousHandler (line 122). For a MAIN-thread crash (the common case), the main thread IS the crashed thread executing the handler chain; once the handler returns, the thread dies / RuntimeInit terminates the process, so the posted Runnable never executes — the crash screen never shows. For a background-thread crash, the delegation chain ends in Android's default handler which calls Process.killProcess(), racing (and usually beating) the main-looper Runnable. The KDoc claims CrashActivity is 'queued' before the system flow, but a queued Runnable does not survive process death. Net effect: the entire CrashActivity recovery feature is effectively unreachable, and the user only sees the system 'App keeps stopping' dialog. Secondary: each crash is recorded multiple times — CrashReporter.recordException (non-fatal) in the handler, Crashlytics' own fatal record via its wrapped handler, and (if CrashActivity ever did launch) a third synthetic RuntimeException(trace) record in CrashActivity.onCreate — polluting Crashlytics dedup/grouping.
evidence: Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).post { CrashActivity.start(this@MyApp, stack) } ... previousHandler?.uncaughtException(thread, throwable) — the default handler terminates the process synchronously before the posted Runnable can run; for main-thread crashes the looper is already dead.
suggestedFix: Start CrashActivity synchronously from the crashing thread (the Intent already carries FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK | FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK), then terminate the process explicitly (Process.killProcess(Process.myPid()); exitProcess(10)) instead of delegating to the default handler — or adopt a dedicated-process crash-screen approach. Decide whether the additional recordException in CrashActivity should be dropped to avoid double-counting.
verifierNote: MyApp.kt:115-122 verified: for a main-thread crash the handler runs after Looper.loop() has thrown out, so the Runnable posted to the dead main looper never executes and the delegation chain ends in the system KillApplicationHandler killing the process — CrashActivity is unreachable in the dominant crash case. One sub-claim is overstated: for a background-thread crash the system dialog blocks the crashed thread before killProcess, so the live main looper may actually launch CrashActivity; this doesn't change the headline, severity, or fix. Triple-recording also verified (handler recordException + Crashlytics fatal wrap + CrashActivity.kt:54 synthetic RuntimeException).

title: System gesture exclusion rect is never cleared on dispose and clobbers the whole root view's exclusion list
evidence: Modifier.onGloballyPositioned { coords -> view.systemGestureExclusionRects = listOf(Rect(...)) } — LocalView.current is the single root AndroidComposeView in this single-activity app; there is no DisposableEffect/onDispose resetting the list to emptyList().
detail: The modifier sets view.systemGestureExclusionRects on the root AndroidComposeView from onGloballyPositioned but (a) never clears it when the fast scroller leaves composition, and (b) REPLACES the entire list, so two simultaneous users of the modifier would overwrite each other. Because the root view outlives navigation, after visiting any screen with LazyVerticalScrollerWithScrollBar (e.g. Library) a stale edge-band where the scrollbar thumb used to be keeps suppressing the system back-swipe gesture on every subsequent screen until something else overwrites it. The commonMain expect KDoc (FastScrollerGestureExclusion.kt:10) also claims the Android actual 'delegates to Modifier.systemGestureExclusion() (API 29+)' — it does not; the foundation modifier would have handled per-node add/remove and disposal correctly.
suggestedFix: Replace the hand-rolled implementation with androidx.compose.foundation.systemGestureExclusion() (which scopes the rect to the layout node and removes it on detach), or wrap in Modifier.composed with a DisposableEffect that restores/clears the previous exclusion rect list on dispose and appends instead of replacing.
verifierNote: FastScrollerGestureExclusion.android.kt:18-28 verified: assigns view.systemGestureExclusionRects (whole-list replace) on LocalView (the root AndroidComposeView, which outlives navigation) from onGloballyPositioned with no DisposableEffect cleanup — the stale thumb-band rect keeps suppressing the system back-swipe on later screens until overwritten. The commonMain expect KDoc (FastScrollerGestureExclusion.kt:10) indeed falsely claims delegation to Modifier.systemGestureExclusion(); consumer at LazyVerticalScrollerWithScrollBar.kt:249. Suggested foundation-modifier fix is real and handles attach/detach correctly.

title: CrashActivity is exported=true with no intent-filter — unnecessarily launchable by third-party apps
detail: CrashActivity is only ever started from inside the app (MyApp's uncaught handler), yet it is declared android:exported="true". Any installed app can launch it with an arbitrary extra_stacktrace string: the activity will then call FirebaseCrashlytics.recordException(RuntimeException(attackerText)) + sendUnsentReports() (polluting crash analytics with attacker-controlled reports) and render attacker-controlled text full-screen under the app's identity. It needs no exported access: an activity without an intent-filter is still reachable via explicit intent from the same app when exported=false. The native manifest has the same exported=true (parity), but it is mildly harmful and free to fix.
evidence: <activity android:name=".crash.CrashActivity" android:exported="true" ...> with no <intent-filter>; CrashActivity.onCreate reads intent.getStringExtra(EXTRA_STACKTRACE) and records it to Crashlytics.
suggestedFix: Change to android:exported="false" — in-app explicit launches via CrashActivity.start() keep working unchanged.
verifierNote: AndroidManifest.xml:50-54 declares CrashActivity exported=true with no intent-filter; CrashActivity.kt:50-56 records attacker-supplied extra_stacktrace to Crashlytics. Only launcher is in-app CrashActivity.start() (MyApp uncaught handler), which works with exported=false (explicit same-app intent). Native has the same exported=true, but APP_MAP allows noting parity items that are harmful; manifest-only fix, no user-visible change.

title: Notification cover fetch uses URL.openConnection() with no timeouts and no per-source headers
detail: showChapterNotification loads the manga cover via URL(notification.mangaImageUrl).openConnection().getInputStream() — URLConnection's default connect/read timeouts are infinite, so a stalled host hangs the coroutine (and an IO-dispatcher thread) forever; up to 6 of these can be in flight per refresh. It also bypasses the app's configured HTTP stack entirely: no cf_clearance/User-Agent/Referer headers are sent, so covers from Cloudflare-protected sources (most of the catalog) will reliably 403 and the notification silently loses its large icon (runCatching swallows it). Best-effort is fine, but unbounded hangs are not.
evidence: runCatching { val url = URL(notification.mangaImageUrl); BitmapFactory.decodeStream(url.openConnection().getInputStream()) }.getOrNull() — no setConnectTimeout/setReadTimeout, no headers.
suggestedFix: Set explicit connect/read timeouts (e.g. 10s) on the URLConnection, or reuse the existing OkHttp/Coil pipeline (which already injects per-source headers) to fetch the cover bytes.
verifierNote: ChapterNotificationHelper.kt:130-133: URL(...).openConnection().getInputStream() with no setConnectTimeout/setReadTimeout and no headers; up to 6 launches per refresh (line 118). URLConnection default timeouts are infinite, so the unbounded-hang claim is correct Java semantics; runCatching swallows the 403 case.

title: Helper scope lacks SupervisorJob and showChapterNotification's launch body is unguarded
detail: coroutineScope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) creates a scope with a plain Job. addNewChapterNotification's launch is fully try/caught, but showChapterNotification's launch body is not: if notificationManager.notify(...) or getString(...) throws, the exception (1) cancels the scope's Job, permanently killing all future chapter notifications for the process lifetime, and (2) propagates to the default CoroutineExceptionHandler → Thread uncaught handler → crashes the whole app from a background notification fan-out. Low probability per call, but the failure mode is app-wide.
evidence: private val coroutineScope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) ... private fun showChapterNotification(...) { coroutineScope.launch { ... notificationManager?.notify(notification.id.toInt(), builder.build()) } } — no try/catch, no SupervisorJob.
suggestedFix: Use CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) and wrap showChapterNotification's launch body in try/catch logging the error (matching the addNewChapterNotification pattern).
verifierNote: ChapterNotificationHelper.kt:53 CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) gets a plain Job; showChapterNotification's launch body (127-147) has no try/catch (only the bitmap fetch is runCatching-wrapped). An exception from notify()/getString() in a root coroutine hits the default handler -> Android process crash, and cancels the scope. Correct coroutine semantics; fix mirrors the existing addNewChapterNotification guard.

title: CbzMigrationWorker is registered in Koin but never enqueued anywhere; KDoc claims a Settings trigger that doesn't exist
detail: The KDoc says 'the storage-cleanup feature in Settings can enqueue it as a one-time OneTimeWorkRequest'. So the worker (and its workerOf binding in AppKoinModule.kt:35 plus the me.manga.yamiapk.work.** proguard keep) is dead code with a misleading KDoc. Secondary: the catch (t: Throwable) at line 58 also swallows CancellationException (contract §9/§10 says CE must be rethrown), logging worker cancellation as 'CBZ migration failed'.

suggestedFix: Either delete the worker + its workerOf binding (Settings already covers the migration inline), or wire the documented Settings enqueue. If kept, rethrow CancellationException in the catch.

title: DisposableEffect(webView, url) destroys the remembered WebView on url change and then reuses the destroyed instance; callbacks are captured once at creation
detail: The WebView is created in remember(context) (lives for the whole composition), but the load effect is keyed on (webView, url): if the url parameter ever changes while the host stays composed, the old effect's onDispose calls webView.stopLoading(); webView.destroy(), and the re-run then calls loadUrl on a DESTROYED WebView — permanently dead browser (and destroy() is invoked while the view is still attached via AndroidView). Additionally the WebViewClient/WebChromeClient built inside remember capture the FIRST composition's onPageFinished / onCookiesAvailable / onUserAgentResolved / allowNavigation lambdas and the userAgent value; later recompositions passing new lambdas/UA are silently ignored (no rememberUpdatedState). Current callers (WebViewScreenRoute, CF 403 solver) pass a fixed url per back-stack entry, so this is latent rather than user-visible today — but it's a trap for the next caller.
evidence: val webView = remember(context) { WebView(context).apply { ... webViewClient = object : WebViewClient() { ... onPageFinished(resolved) ... } } } ... DisposableEffect(webView, url) { webView.loadUrl(url); onDispose { webView.stopLoading(); webView.destroy() } }
suggestedFix: Split the effects: DisposableEffect(webView) owns destroy() (in AndroidView's onRelease ideally), LaunchedEffect(url) calls loadUrl. Hold the callback parameters in rememberUpdatedState and read them through the state inside the client overrides.
verifierNote: WebViewHost.android.kt: WebView built in remember(context) (36) with clients capturing first-composition lambdas/UA; DisposableEffect(webView, url) (117-123) destroys the remembered instance on url change then the re-run calls loadUrl on the destroyed WebView. Correctly framed as latent (current callers pass a fixed url per back-stack entry).

title: hasPermission is only computed once — granting POST_NOTIFICATIONS from system settings is not reflected until the screen is recreated
detail: The MutableStateFlow seed is computed in remember { } at first composition, and is only updated by the in-app permission launcher callback. The interface also exposes openAppSettings(); if the user (typical after a permanent denial) grants the permission in system settings and returns to the app, hasPermission keeps reporting false — UI that gates on it (theme/onboarding notification row) stays in the 'denied' state until the composable is recreated. There is no ON_RESUME re-check.
evidence: val hasPermission = remember { MutableStateFlow(hasPostNotificationPermission(app)) } — no LifecycleEventObserver/ON_RESUME refresh after openAppSettings() round-trip.
suggestedFix: Observe Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME (LifecycleResumeEffect / LifecycleEventObserver) and re-run hasPostNotificationPermission(app) into the flow so a settings-granted permission is picked up on return.
verifierNote: RememberNotificationPermissionRequester.android.kt:113 seeds the flow once in remember{}; only the launcher callback (118) and pre-T request() (130) ever write it; no ON_RESUME observer exists despite openAppSettings() (134-140) inviting a settings round-trip. remember{} does not recompute on recomposition, so the stale-grant claim is correct Compose semantics.

title: Hostname verification disabled for *.s3.wasabisys.com on the Coil image client
detail: The hostnameVerifier returns true unconditionally for any hostname ending in .s3.wasabisys.com. The cert chain must still be CA-trusted, but hostname verification is what binds a cert to the host — with it bypassed, a MITM presenting ANY valid certificate (for any domain they own) is accepted for image traffic to those hosts. This is a deliberate native-parity port (native CoilModule did the same because Wasabi bucket certs mismatch), so it's an owner decision, but it weakens TLS for that whole CDN suffix. Worst case here is image substitution/observation rather than credential theft.
evidence: .hostnameVerifier { hostname, session -> if (hostname.endsWith(".s3.wasabisys.com")) { true } else { HttpsURLConnection.getDefaultHostnameVerifier().verify(hostname, session) } }
suggestedFix: Tighten the bypass: instead of blanket-accepting, verify the presented cert's SANs match *.wasabisys.com (i.e. accept the known wildcard-mismatch shape only), or pin the Wasabi CA for those hosts. Keep behavior change behind owner sign-off (native parity).
verifierNote: PlatformNetworkFetcher.android.kt:95-101: hostnameVerifier returns true unconditionally for *.s3.wasabisys.com — any CA-valid cert for any domain passes for those hosts. Deliberate native-parity port (KDoc cites native CoilModule.kt:37-47); harmful enough to flag under the parity rule, image-substitution blast radius keeps it minor; behavior change needs owner sign-off -> risky correct.

title: Static-analysis job downloads and executes unverified binaries from GitHub releases
detail: The advisory static-analysis job curls the ktlint executable and the detekt-cli zip and runs them with no checksum/signature verification. A compromised release asset (or MITM, though HTTPS mitigates) would execute arbitrary code in CI with checkout access. The job has no secrets exposed and is continue-on-error, so blast radius is limited, but pinning a SHA-256 check is cheap hardening consistent with the rest of the workflow's care.
evidence: curl -sSLO https://github.com/pinterest/ktlint/releases/download/1.5.0/ktlint; chmod +x ktlint; ./ktlint ... and the analogous detekt-cli download/unzip/run.
suggestedFix: Add a sha256sum -c verification against pinned digests for both downloads before executing them.
verifierNote: ci.yml:155 and ci.yml:164 curl ktlint/detekt-cli and execute with no checksum; job has no secrets and is continue-on-error, so minor is right. sha256 pin is a one-line additive hardening.

title: Registration test cannot actually fail on duplicate definitions — Koin 4.x silently overrides by default
detail: The test KDoc (and MyApp's KDoc, 'Duplicate-binding diagnostics fire here at startup') claims that a type bound twice 'surfaces here as a registration failure'. With Koin 4.2.0, KoinApplication.modules(...) loads with allowOverride = true by default: a duplicate definition silently replaces the earlier one (at most a log line), and koinApplication { } does not throw. So this test only proves the module blocks execute without throwing — it provides no duplicate-binding guarantee, giving false confidence for exactly the Platform-Cutover rebinding regressions it was written to guard.
evidence: val app = koinApplication { modules(allSharedModules() + platformModule() + allReworkModules() + appKoinModule) } — no createEagerInstances/verify, no allowOverride(false).
suggestedFix: Load modules with override disallowed in the test (e.g. koinApplication { allowOverride(false); modules(...) } — Koin 4's KoinApplication.allowOverride(false) makes duplicate definitions throw DefinitionOverrideException) and update both KDocs.
verifierNote: Verified against Koin 4.2.0 sources in the Gradle cache: KoinApplication.kt:40 'private var allowOverride = true', modules() loads with that flag, and InstanceRegistry.saveMapping throws DefinitionOverrideException only when allowOverride=false (else logs a warning). So the test (KoinGraphRegistrationTest.kt:27-29) cannot fail on duplicates as its KDoc claims; suggested allowOverride(false) API exists (KoinApplication.kt:95).

The variable is dead state and the cancel is dead code; if the cancellation was intended (to abort an in-flight cleanup when a new one starts), it never worked.

title: Bitmap.compress() return value ignored — failed encode returns truncated bytes instead of the documented null
detail: The file's contract (and the expect KDoc) says 'Returns null on any failure'. Bitmap.compress signals failure by returning false WITHOUT throwing; the code ignores the boolean and returns stream.toByteArray() regardless, so a failed compress yields an empty/partial byte array that the share path will hand to the share sheet as a corrupt PNG instead of silently no-opping.
evidence: bitmap.asAndroidBitmap().compress(Bitmap.CompressFormat.PNG, 100, stream); stream.toByteArray() — compress's Boolean result is discarded.
suggestedFix: Check the result: val ok = bitmap.asAndroidBitmap().compress(...); if (!ok) return@runCatching null (or throw) so the caller gets null on failure.
verifierNote: ImageBitmapPngEncoder.android.kt:20-21: compress()'s Boolean is discarded and stream.toByteArray() is returned regardless, contradicting the file's own 'Returns null on any failure' contract (KDoc line 15-16). Bitmap.compress signals failure via false without throwing, so runCatching does not help. Accurate.

title: Main-frame host pin is bypassable via bare suffix match; the two correct clauses are dead code
detail: isAllowed() returns `targetHost == host || targetHost.endsWith(".$host") || targetHost.endsWith(host)`. The third clause subsumes the first two (any exact match or dot-boundary subdomain also satisfies a bare endsWith), so the effective rule is a bare string-suffix match. A registrable lookalike domain such as `evil-lek-manga.net` ends with `lek-manga.net` and passes the pin without being the host or a subdomain, defeating the sandbox's stated purpose (GAP-WV-01: keep the Cloudflare-challenge WebView's main frame on the host whose cf_clearance cookie is being captured). On ad-heavy scraper sites a main-frame redirect to a lookalike host is a realistic attack, and the user is mid-anti-bot-challenge, i.e. primed to interact. The KDoc says the bare endsWith deliberately mirrors the legacy Android rule, and the author also wrote the correct dot-boundary clause — so this is a parity-vs-security decision for the owner: dropping the third clause makes the first two meaningful and closes the bypass, at the cost of diverging from native.
evidence: return targetHost == host || targetHost.endsWith(".$host") || targetHost.endsWith(host)  // clause 3 makes clauses 1-2 unreachable as distinct checks; "evil-lek-manga.net".endsWith("lek-manga.net") == true
suggestedFix: Drop the trailing `|| targetHost.endsWith(host)` so only exact host or dot-boundary subdomains pass: `return targetHost == host || targetHost.endsWith(".$host")`. If strict native parity must be kept, at minimum document the bypass and remove the two dead clauses so the rule reads as what it is.
verifierNote: WebViewUrlSandbox.kt:51 verified: the trailing `targetHost.endsWith(host)` subsumes the exact-match and dot-boundary clauses, so the effective rule is a bare suffix match and `evil-lek-manga.net`.endsWith("lek-manga.net") passes the pin — claim correct, and the KDoc confirms it deliberately mirrors the legacy rule (parity-vs-security owner call, harmful enough to report under the ground rules). fixSafety corrected report-only->risky: the file is not in a report-only path; the fix is a deliberate behavior change diverging from native, which is exactly the 'risky' bucket. Not critical: it's a weakened defense-in-depth pin, not direct data loss.

title: toRelativeString always renders English month names, diverging from native's locale-aware date format in a 10-locale (RTL Arabic-heavy) app
detail: displayFormatter hardcodes MonthNames.ENGLISH_ABBREVIATED, so dates older than yesterday render like 'Jun 5, 2026' in every locale, while the 'Today'/'Yesterday' branches of the same function ARE localized via stringResource. The native spec (native-app .../core/util/date/Date.kt:17) used DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMM d, yyyy") with the default locale, which localizes month names (e.g. Arabic). The mixed output (localized relative words + English absolute dates) is inconsistent for the app's primary Arabic audience. Note: timeAgo()'s `seconds < 0 -> ""` IS native parity (native line 28) and is not a finding.
evidence: private val displayFormatter = LocalDate.Format { monthName(MonthNames.ENGLISH_ABBREVIATED) ... } vs native this.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMM d, yyyy"))
suggestedFix: Localize the month names — e.g. a per-locale month-name array in compose-resources fed into LocalDate.Format, or format month via the platform locale on each target. Needs a small design decision since kotlinx-datetime has no built-in localized month names.
verifierNote: The English-month hardcoding at Date.kt:44 vs native's locale-aware DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMM d, yyyy") is real, but zero imports of me.manga.yamiapk.core.util.date exist anywhere — this composeApp Date object is dead code with no user-visible impact. The live divergence moved to the :ui ports (ui/.../details/DetailsScreen.kt MONTH_ABBREVIATIONS English table ~line 2310). Fix should target the :ui port and/or delete this dead file.

title: Reader 403->WebView auto-retry latch cannot fire: plain remember state is destroyed while the WebView destination is on top
detail: rememberReaderCloudflareChallengeSolver stores the pending-retry latch in `remember { mutableStateOf(false) }` and watches `currentBackStackEntryFlow` from a LaunchedEffect, both inside the Reader destination's composition. Navigation-Compose only keeps the CURRENT destination composed: when safeNavigate(Screen.WebView) pushes the WebView, the Reader route leaves composition, the LaunchedEffect is cancelled and the plain-remember latch is forgotten (only rememberSaveable survives via the NavHost SaveableStateHolder). On pop-back the route recomposes fresh with pendingRetry=false, so the armed one-shot OnRetry never fires. ReaderViewModel's OnEnter re-entry idempotence means the re-mount does not refetch either, so the user returns from solving the Cloudflare challenge to the same error pane and must tap Retry manually — the advertised 'auto-retry-on-return' (Reader parity item #6) is dead on all platforms. Same defect in the Details twin (code-ac-2) and in ChapterImagesByLegacyArgsReworkScreenRoute which reuses this helper.
evidence: var pendingRetry by remember { mutableStateOf(false) } ... LaunchedEffect(readerEntry) { navController.currentBackStackEntryFlow.filter { it == readerEntry }.collect { if (pendingRetry) { pendingRetry = false; onRetry() } } } — the comment claims it 'Survives recomposition (remember)' but it does not survive leaving composition, which is exactly what happens while the WebView is open.
suggestedFix: Change the latch to `rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }`. On return, the saved `true` is restored, the restarted LaunchedEffect immediately receives the current entry from currentBackStackEntryFlow (replay=1), and onRetry fires exactly once. Also fixes config-change and process-death cases.
verifierNote: ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute.kt:191 verified: pendingRetry is a plain `remember` inside the Reader destination's composition; NavHost composes only the current destination, so pushing Screen.WebView disposes the Reader composition (only rememberSaveable survives via the SaveableStateHolder), cancelling the LaunchedEffect and forgetting the armed latch — on pop-back it recomposes with false and OnRetry never fires; the VM's documented OnEnter re-entry guard (same route KDoc) prevents a refetch on remount. rememberSaveable fix works because currentBackStackEntryFlow is a replay-1 shared flow that immediately re-delivers the reader entry to the restarted collector.

title: Search overlay 'Open in WebView' opens a blank page: navigates Screen.WebView with url="" and nothing resolves the blank URL from the api
detail: The Search error-state action navigates `Screen.WebView(url = "", api = homeState.activeTab?.api.orEmpty())`, with a comment claiming 'the Screen.WebView route resolving the concrete source landing URL from the api'. title: Onboarding 'enable notifications' toast fires the moment the permission dialog opens, before the user has answered (native toasts only on actual denial)
detail: The toast LaunchedEffect is keyed on (hasPermission, autoRequested.value) with condition `autoRequested.value && !hasPermission`. On every Android 13+ fresh install: hasPermission starts false, the auto-request effect flips autoRequested to true and launches the system dialog; the recomposition immediately re-runs the toast effect with (false, true) and the condition is already true — so the 'you need to enable notifications' toast shows while the system permission dialog is still on screen and even if the user then GRANTS. The native parity spec (native-app ThemeSelectionScreen.kt:69-72) shows this toast only inside the ActivityResult callback when granted == false, i.e. after a real denial. The KDoc's claim that the transition 'auto-requested but denied is what triggers the toast' does not match the code: there is no signal distinguishing 'request in flight' from 'denied' (a denial leaves hasPermission false->false, producing no new state change, so an actual denial after the premature toast shows nothing further). The native shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale -> openAppSettings redirect on permanent denial is also dropped even though the requester interface exposes openAppSettings().
evidence: LaunchedEffect(hasPermission, autoRequested.value) { if (autoRequested.value && !hasPermission) toastShower.showLong(deniedMessage) } — runs immediately after the sibling LaunchedEffect(Unit) sets autoRequested.value = true and calls request(); the user has not yet interacted with the dialog. Native: launcher callback `{ granted -> if (!granted) Toast... }`.
suggestedFix: Surface the denial from the request result instead of inferring it from state: extend NotificationPermissionRequester (or add a result callback to request()) so the route toasts only when the launcher callback reports granted == false; optionally restore the openAppSettings redirect on permanent denial for native parity.
verifierNote: Verified: ThemeSelectionScreenRoute.kt:155-166 — LaunchedEffect(Unit) sets autoRequested=true and calls request(); the recomposition relaunches the toast effect with (hasPermission=false, autoRequested=true), firing the denial toast while the Android 13+ system dialog is still open, even if the user grants. A real denial then sets the MutableStateFlow false->false (RememberNotificationPermissionRequester.android.kt:117-118, conflated, no emission) so no toast fires on actual denial. Native parity confirmed at native-app ThemeSelectionScreen.kt:68-78 (toast only in launcher callback on !granted, plus shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale->settings redirect; openAppSettings() exists unused at the android actual :134). Fix requires extending the requester contract across 3 actuals — risky is correct.

title: Page-share PNG encode runs synchronously on the main thread
detail: onSharePage calls encodeImageBitmapToPng(bitmap) directly in the callback (main thread) and only the subsequent shareBitmapBytes is suspend (its Android impl hops to Dispatchers.IO for the file write). PNG compression at quality 100 of a captured manga page — pages are tall, often multi-megapixel webtoon strips per the domain risk profile — can block the UI thread for hundreds of milliseconds or more, causing a visible freeze on every share tap. The identical pattern exists in ChapterImagesByLegacyArgsReworkScreenRoute.kt:151. A null encode also silently no-ops with zero user feedback (documented as intentional, but combined with the freeze the action can appear dead).
evidence: onSharePage = { bitmap -> val bytes = encodeImageBitmapToPng(bitmap); if (bytes != null) { shareScope.launch { screenshotProvider.shareBitmapBytes(bytes, "Share screenshot") } } } — encode happens before entering the coroutine.
suggestedFix: Move the encode inside the coroutine on a background dispatcher: shareScope.launch { val bytes = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { encodeImageBitmapToPng(bitmap) }; if (bytes != null) screenshotProvider.shareBitmapBytes(bytes, "Share screenshot") }. Apply to both reader route adapters.
verifierNote: ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute.kt:154-156: encodeImageBitmapToPng(bitmap) runs in the click callback (main thread) before shareScope.launch; only shareBitmapBytes is suspend. Identical at ChapterImagesByLegacyArgsReworkScreenRoute.kt:151-157. PNG@100 encode of a captured page bitmap on main thread is a real jank source; moving it inside the coroutine on a background dispatcher is behavior-preserving.

title: runCatching around ensureSiteInitialized swallows CancellationException inside LaunchedEffect
detail: In the api-keyed rememberSourceImageRequest overload, the LaunchedEffect body wraps the suspending repo.ensureSiteInitialized() in runCatching. runCatching catches CancellationException too, so when the composable leaves composition mid-init the cancellation is eaten and the next line (headersSnapshot = repo.defaultHeaders) still executes in a cancelled coroutine. Impact is contained (the effect ends right after, the state write targets a disposed composition), but it violates the project's own rule that CancellationException is always re-thrown, and it hides genuine init failures from any future logging.
evidence: LaunchedEffect(repo) { if (repo is BaseManga && headersSnapshot.isEmpty()) { runCatching { repo.ensureSiteInitialized() }; headersSnapshot = repo.defaultHeaders } }
suggestedFix: Replace runCatching with try/catch that re-throws CancellationException: `try { repo.ensureSiteInitialized() } catch (c: CancellationException) { throw c } catch (_: Throwable) { /* headers stay empty; raw-URL fallback */ }` before reading repo.defaultHeaders.
verifierNote: SourceImageRequest.kt:92: runCatching { repo.ensureSiteInitialized() } inside LaunchedEffect does catch CancellationException (runCatching catches Throwable), violating the project's re-throw rule, then executes the state write in a cancelled coroutine. Impact is contained (write targets a disposed composition) — minor is correct; the suggested try/catch fix compiles (needs the CancellationException import).

title: search() and featured() silently ignore the page parameter
detail: MangaSourceClient.search(query, page) and featured(page) take a page number, but the adapter always calls repo.fetchSearchDataF(SearchType.Normal(query)) / repo.fetchPopularManga(baseUrl) — page is dropped (home() does honor page via fetchMoreManga). Today every caller passes page = 1 (SearchRepositoryImpl:83/120, HomeFeedRepositoryImpl:187), so behavior is correct, but the contract is a latent trap: if search/featured pagination is ever wired (the generic configs and FallbackSourceClient already pass page through), the legacy adapter/fallback will return page-1 results again as a wrong-but-Success, which both duplicates rows and suppresses any diagnosis. Note legacy BaseMangaRepository exposes no paged-search API, so an honest fix needs an owner decision (e.g. return Failure for page > 1, or extend the legacy surface).

title: KCEFClient is allocated per WebViewHost mount but never disposed (native CEF client leak)
detail: Each composition of WebViewHost calls KCEF.newClientOrNullBlocking inside remember(kcefInitialized). Verified against the KCEF 2025.03.23 sources: every call executes cefApp.createClient() and the KCEFClient init block creates and registers an internal CefMessageRouter ('cefQueryEvaluate'), i.e. it allocates fresh native CEF resources per call. The DisposableEffect at lines 224-232 closes the browser (close(true)) and disposes the app-side uaRouter, but never calls client.dispose() (KCEFClient.kt:274 exposes it). The Desktop WebView screen is the Cloudflare-challenge solver path, which users open repeatedly for CF-walled sources, so clients (each with a registered native message router) accumulate until full app exit. The class KDoc (lines 71-73) claims 'The shared KCEFClient is disposed only on full KCEF teardown ... since reusing a single client across multiple browser instances is cheaper than allocating per-host' — but the code does NOT reuse a single client; it allocates per-host, so the stated rationale for skipping disposal is false.
evidence: val client: KCEFClient? = remember(kcefInitialized) { if (kcefInitialized) KCEF.newClientOrNullBlocking { it?.printStackTrace() } else null } ... onDispose { browser.close(true); client.removeMessageRouter(uaRouter); uaRouter.dispose() } // no client.dispose(). KCEF sources: newClientOrNullBlocking -> KCEFClient(cefApp.createClient()); KCEFClient.init registers its own CefMessageRouter; KCEFClient.dispose() exists.
suggestedFix: Either (a) dispose the per-mount client: in the final DisposableEffect's onDispose, after browser.close(true) and uaRouter.dispose(), call client.dispose(); or (b) actually implement the documented design — hold one process-wide KCEFClient (e.g. lazily in KcefState) and reuse it across mounts. Update the class KDoc to match whichever is chosen.
verifierNote: Claim is correct — verified against KCEF 2025.03.23 sources (KCEF.kt:233 newClientOrNull -> KCEFClient(cefApp.createClient()); KCEFClient init registers an internal 'cefQueryEvaluate' CefMessageRouter; dispose() at KCEFClient.kt:274) and WebViewHost.desktop.kt:224-232 never calls client.dispose(); the class KDoc's shared-client rationale (lines 71-73) is false. Downgraded major->minor: it is a bounded per-screen-visit native resource leak on Windows/Linux only (macOS never creates a client), reclaimed at app exit by KCEF.disposeBlocking (Main.kt:206-208) — no user-visible incorrectness.

title: First-paint loading overlay is non-functional: non-snapshot read of browser.url, sibling (not overlay) layout, and AWT z-order
detail: The trailing `if (browser.url.isNullOrBlank()) { Box(...) { CircularProgressIndicator() } }` cannot work as an overlay: (1) browser.url is a plain JCEF getter, not snapshot state — when the first URL commits, no recomposition is triggered, so the condition is only ever re-evaluated by unrelated recompositions (spinner can linger or never clear deterministically); (2) the Box is emitted as a SIBLING of SwingPanel, so whether it overlays at all depends on the caller's container (the only call site, WebViewComposeScreen.kt:329, places WebViewHost in a Column-like container with Modifier.fillMaxSize — the second sibling gets zero space); (3) even in a Box parent, SwingPanel is a heavyweight AWT component that renders above Compose content, so the spinner would be hidden anyway. Net effect: dead UI code that suggests a loading affordance that never shows.
evidence:
SwingPanel(factory = { browser.uiComponent }, modifier = modifier.fillMaxSize())
if (browser.url.isNullOrBlank()) { Box(modifier = modifier.fillMaxSize(), contentAlignment = Alignment.Center) { CircularProgressIndicator() } }
suggestedFix: Remove the block (the screen already has its own LinearProgressIndicator driven by the controller's isLoading state), or drive a real overlay from DesktopWebViewController.state.isLoading inside a shared Box parent — noting the AWT z-order limitation makes a Compose overlay above SwingPanel ineffective regardless.

title: Browser disposal is keyed on uaRouter: a churning onUserAgentResolved lambda would force-close the live browser without recreating it
detail: DisposableEffect(browser, uaRouter) performs browser.close(true) in onDispose. uaRouter is remember(client, onUserAgentResolved) — keyed on a caller-supplied lambda. If a caller ever passes a non-remembered lambda, every recomposition creates a new router, which re-runs this DisposableEffect and force-closes the browser — while the browser `remember(client, url, allowNavigation)` key did NOT change, so the closed browser stays remembered and mounted in SwingPanel (dead web view). Today the only call site (WebViewComposeScreen.kt:323-328) wraps all callbacks in remember, so this is latent, but the coupling between an unrelated key (uaRouter) and the browser's native lifecycle is a trap. Additionally each new router would be added to the client without removing the previous one until dispose.
evidence: val uaRouter: CefMessageRouter = remember(client, onUserAgentResolved) { ... } ... DisposableEffect(browser, uaRouter) { onDispose { browser.close(true); client.removeMessageRouter(uaRouter); uaRouter.dispose() } }
suggestedFix: Split into two effects: DisposableEffect(browser) { onDispose { browser.close(true) } } and DisposableEffect(client, uaRouter) { onDispose { client.removeMessageRouter(uaRouter); uaRouter.dispose() } }, so browser lifetime is tied only to the browser key.
verifierNote: WebViewHost.desktop.kt:125 keys uaRouter on the caller-supplied onUserAgentResolved lambda and :224-232 keys browser.close(true) on (browser, uaRouter) - a churning lambda would dispose/restart the effect and force-close the still-remembered browser (its remember key at :153 unchanged). Latent today: the sole call site remembers all callbacks (WebViewComposeScreen.kt:319-327). Splitting into two DisposableEffects compiles and preserves behavior.

title: Locale.setDefault() mutates process-global state during composition (not in a SideEffect)
detail: LocalAppLocale.provides() executes Locale.setDefault(locale) and assigns the `default` backing var directly in the composition phase. Compose compositions can be speculative/abandoned; a discarded composition would still have mutated the JVM-global default locale. This mirrors the community-standard compose-resources locale-switch pattern (the keyed recomposition depends on the default being set before resource resolution in the same pass), so it is likely intentional, but it remains a composition side effect on global state worth an owner decision (e.g. comparing against the current default before setting, or documenting the constraint).
evidence: @Composable actual infix fun provides(value: String?): ProvidedValue<*> { if (default == null) default = Locale.getDefault(); val locale = ...; Locale.setDefault(locale); return LocalAppLocale.provides(locale.toLanguageTag()) }
suggestedFix: Document the deliberate composition-phase mutation, and guard with `if (Locale.getDefault() != locale) Locale.setDefault(locale)` to make repeated/speculative compositions idempotent.
verifierNote: Claim is accurate: LocalAppLocale.desktop.kt:27-30 calls Locale.setDefault inside the composition phase (the community-standard compose-resources pattern, almost certainly intentional). fixSafety corrected report-only->safe: the file is not in a forbidden path and the suggested doc note + 'if (Locale.getDefault() != locale)' idempotency guard is behavior-preserving.

title: iOS io dispatcher routes to Dispatchers.Default on an outdated premise — Dispatchers.IO is public on Kotlin/Native since coroutines 1.7.0
detail: The file (and the expect KDoc in core/src/commonMain/.../IoDispatcher.kt, plus DispatcherProvider.kt line 109) claims 'Dispatchers.IO is internal on Kotlin/Native (coroutines 1.9.0)' and cites issue #3205. That issue was the feature request, and it was IMPLEMENTED in coroutines 1.7.0: verified against the kotlinx.coroutines 1.9.0 native sources (the project pins coroutines 1.9.0) — `kotlinx-coroutines-core/native/src/Dispatchers.kt` declares `@Suppress("EXTENSION_SHADOWED_BY_MEMBER") public actual val Dispatchers.IO: CoroutineDispatcher get() = IO` (the member is internal, the extension is public, backed by DefaultIoScheduler with an elastic 64-thread pool). So the iOS actual could bind the real IO pool. As written, every `DispatcherProvider.io` consumer on iOS (rework :data repos' withContext wraps, ReaderViewModel off-main work) shares the cores-limited Default pool with CPU work; blocking IO there can starve CPU-bound work. Impact today is bounded (Ktor Darwin is async, Room KMP manages its own connection pool), which is why this is minor rather than major — but the documented premise for the divergence is simply wrong on the pinned coroutines version.
evidence: actual val platformIoDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default  // comment: "Dispatchers.IO is internal on Kotlin/Native (coroutines 1.9.0)" — but 1.9.0 ships `public actual val Dispatchers.IO` on Native (extension, import kotlinx.coroutines.IO).
suggestedFix: Change the iOS actual to `actual val platformIoDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO` with `import kotlinx.coroutines.IO`, and update the stale claims in IoDispatcher.kt / DispatcherProvider.kt KDoc (and eventually CLAUDE.md, which repeats it). Gate with the iOS compile check.
verifierNote: Core claim verified against the pinned dependency itself: kotlinx-coroutines-core-iosarm64-1.9.0-sources.jar nativeMain/Dispatchers.kt:49 declares `public actual val Dispatchers.IO: CoroutineDispatcher get() = IO` (public since 1.7.0), so IoDispatcher.ios.kt:6-9's 'internal on Kotlin/Native' premise is wrong on the pinned version (CLAUDE.md repeats it). fixSafety corrected safe->risky: rebinding the iOS io dispatcher from Default to the 64-thread IO pool is a runtime behavior change on a target with no automated runtime gate; the KDoc corrections alone are safe.

title: Stale comment: progress-poll loop claims it 'stops as soon as the page finishes' but runs for the whole composition lifetime
detail: The comment above the LaunchedEffect says the poll runs 'while a navigation is in flight' and 'stops as soon as the page finishes'. The actual loop is `while (coroutineContext.isActive) { iosController.onProgressPoll(webView); delay(100) }` — it polls every 100ms for as long as the composable is composed, regardless of load state. The continuous polling is deliberate (onProgressPoll's KDoc says it is the single source of truth for isLoading/canGoBack/canGoForward, replacing the didStartProvisionalNavigation hook), so the code is right and the comment is wrong. The cost is negligible (StateFlow.update with an equal value dedupes), but the comment misleads a maintainer into thinking there is a stop condition to preserve.
evidence:
// ...we poll the value on a short cadence while a navigation is in flight. The loop suspends cheaply and stops as soon as the page finishes.
 LaunchedEffect(webView) { while (coroutineContext.isActive) { iosController.onProgressPoll(webView); delay(100) } }
suggestedFix: Reword the comment to state the loop polls continuously while the WebView is composed (it also keeps back/forward enablement fresh after in-page navigations) and only ends when the composable leaves composition.
verifierNote: WebViewHost.ios.kt:70-72 comment claims the poll 'stops as soon as the page finishes', but the loop at :74-79 is `while (coroutineContext.isActive) { onProgressPoll; delay(100) }` - it runs for the whole composition. The continuous poll is deliberate (IosWebViewController.onProgressPoll KDoc at :115-121 calls it the single source of truth replacing the colliding didStartProvisionalNavigation hook), so only the comment is wrong.

title: No didFailProvisionalNavigation/didFailNavigation handling — failed page loads leave a silent blank WKWebView
detail: WebViewDelegate only implements decidePolicyForNavigationAction and didFinishNavigation. On a load failure (DNS failure, offline, TLS error — common for the scraped sites this WebView exists to solve Cloudflare for), WKWebView renders nothing for a provisional failure: the user gets a blank white view. The poll loop does clear isLoading (WKWebView.loading flips false), so the progress bar disappears but no error feedback of any kind is shown, and onPageFinished/onCookiesAvailable never fire. Android is better off by accident: android.webkit.WebView renders its own built-in net::ERR_* error page, so the gap is iOS-specific. Given the app's offline/poor-network risk profile (APP_MAP), the CF-solver flow dead-ending in a blank screen is a real, if edge-case, UX hole.
evidence: class WebViewDelegate : NSObject(), WKNavigationDelegateProtocol { override fun webView(webView, decidePolicyForNavigationAction, decisionHandler) ...; override fun webView(webView, didFinishNavigation: WKNavigation?) ... }  // no didFail* overrides
suggestedFix: Implement `webView(_:didFailProvisionalNavigation:withError:)` (and didFailNavigation) on WebViewDelegate to clear loading state via the controller and surface a visible failure (e.g. an error callback up to WebViewComposeScreen, or loading a minimal error page). Note the Kotlin/Native overload-collision constraint that already forced the polling workaround — the didFail* selectors have distinct signatures (they take NSError) so they do not collide.
verifierNote: WebViewHost.ios.kt:170-231: WebViewDelegate implements only decidePolicyForNavigationAction and didFinishNavigation - no didFailProvisionalNavigation/didFailNavigation, so a DNS/offline/TLS failure leaves a blank WKWebView with no feedback (the poll clears isLoading; onPageFinished/onCookiesAvailable never fire). The didFail* selectors take an NSError param so they do not hit the Kotlin/Native overload collision that forced the polling workaround. Real iOS-specific UX hole in the CF-solver flow; minor/risky calibration is right.

title: KDoc on `unconfined` describes the opposite of Dispatchers.Unconfined ('confined single-thread queue ... must be serialized')
detail: The interface doc for `unconfined` reads 'Confined single-thread queue — for code that must be serialized but is otherwise non-blocking.' DefaultDispatcherProvider binds it to Dispatchers.Unconfined, which is NOT confined and provides NO serialization: it runs in the caller's thread until the first suspension and resumes on whatever thread the resuming continuation uses. Any future consumer that follows this doc and uses `unconfined` to serialize access will get a concurrency bug. (Today only tests reference the property, so it is doc-only — but it is a loaded footgun in a foundation module.) The description sounds like it was meant for a `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` confined dispatcher that was never added. Also trivial: line 5 imports `platformIoDispatcher` from the file's own package (redundant import).
evidence:
/** Confined single-thread queue — for code that must be serialized but is otherwise non-blocking. */
    val unconfined: CoroutineDispatcher
...
    override val unconfined: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Unconfined
suggestedFix: Rewrite the KDoc to describe Dispatchers.Unconfined accurately (test/immediate-execution use; no thread confinement), or — if a serialized queue was the intent — add a separate `limitedParallelism(1)`-backed property. Also drop the redundant same-package import on line 5.
verifierNote: DispatcherProvider.kt:93-94 documents `unconfined` as a 'Confined single-thread queue... must be serialized' while :112 binds Dispatchers.Unconfined (no confinement, no serialization - runs in caller thread until first suspension). Grep confirms no production consumer (only test fakes override the property), so doc-only today but a real footgun. Redundant same-package import at line 5 also confirmed.

title: KermitLoggerAdapter.log: dead if/else (both branches identical) and double tag plumbing
detail: The private log() splits on `throwable == null` but both branches make the exact same call (the null branch just passes `throwable = null` explicitly, which is what passing `throwable` would do). The branch is dead weight. Additionally each call does `KermitLogger.withTag(tag).log(..., tag = tag, ...)` — the tag is applied twice (once via the tagged logger instance, once via the explicit parameter). Harmless but redundant; one un-branched call with a single tag mechanism is equivalent.
evidence: if (throwable == null) { KermitLogger.withTag(tag).log(severity = severity, tag = tag, throwable = null, message = message) } else { KermitLogger.withTag(tag).log(severity = severity, tag = tag, throwable = throwable, message = message) }
suggestedFix: Collapse to a single call: `KermitLogger.withTag(tag).log(severity = severity, tag = tag, throwable = throwable, message = message)` (or drop withTag and pass tag once).
verifierNote: Logger.kt:94-100 verified verbatim: both if/else branches make the identical KermitLogger.withTag(tag).log(...) call (null branch passes throwable = null explicitly), and tag is applied twice (withTag + tag param). Collapse to one call is behavior-identical.

title: Every admin mutation re-fetches the entire complaints collection, and the read-modify-write is unguarded (lost-update window); KDoc undersells the cost as 'one extra Firestore READ'
detail: fetchLegacyById calls legacyGetAll() — a collection-wide Firestore fetch (N document reads + full payload transfer) — then firstOrNull{ id }. The KDoc claims 'Cost is one extra Firestore READ per admin action', which mischaracterizes a whole-collection fetch; as the complaints collection grows (user-generated content, per APP_MAP an abuse surface) each status change/closure-reason/edit gets slower and costlier. Separately, the fetch-copy-update sequence is a non-transactional read-modify-write of the whole document: two near-simultaneous admin actions (e.g. changeStatus and addClosureReason) can silently clobber each other's metadata/status. Admin-only and low-frequency, hence minor — and the fix needs the legacy facade to grow a get-by-id (or a field-level update), so it is an owner decision.
evidence: private suspend fun fetchLegacyById(id: String): LegacyComplaint = legacyGetAll().firstOrNull { it.id == id } ?: error("Complaint $id not found")
suggestedFix: Add a get-by-id read to the legacy complaint facade (Firestore document get) and use it here; correct the KDoc cost claim. Optionally move the mutations to field-level updates (or a transaction) to close the lost-update window.
verifierNote: AdminComplaintActionRepositoryImpl.kt:180-182 fetchLegacyById -> legacyGetAll() -> ComplaintFirestoreRestDataSource.getAllComplaints() (GET of the whole collection, N document reads), contradicting the KDoc's 'one extra Firestore READ' (lines 38-39). updateComplaint PATCHes the full document fields with no transaction/updateMask, so the fetch-copy-write lost-update window between concurrent admin actions is real. Admin-only/low-frequency -> minor; fix needs a legacy facade get-by-id -> risky.

title: Both pinned FAQ entries share id="admin" -> duplicate LazyColumn key crashes the Feedback Manager screen
detail: PINNED_COMPLAINTS contains two ComplaintSummary entries with the identical id "admin" (lines 94 and 111). Native carried the same duplicate ids but its screen did not key the list by id, so this is a rework-only crash.

title: Reply to a PINNED FAQ entry always fails: #9 re-fetch cannot find synthetic pinned complaints in Firestore
detail: replyToComplaint now re-fetches the parent via fetchLegacyById(parent.userId, parent.id) before constructing the reply (the #9 metadata-preservation change). Pinned FAQ entries are static in-binary records (userId="0", id="admin") that never exist in Firestore, so getUser("0") returns no matching doc and fetchLegacyById throws `error("Complaint admin not found for user 0")` -> Result.failure -> the user sees an error snackbar. The product intent (PinnedComplaints.kt KDoc and ComplaintActionDialog.kt:106-108: "Reply is always available ... PINNED parents accept replies as a feedback channel") and native behavior (native builds the reply locally from the in-memory parent: ComplaintActionDialog.kt:312 `metadata = (complaint.metadata ?: emptyMap()) + mapOf("replyto" to complaint.id)`, no re-fetch) both expect replying to pinned entries to work. So the reply affordance shown on every pinned entry is permanently broken.
evidence: fetchLegacyById (lines 129-131): `getUser(userId).firstOrNull { it.id == id } ?: error(...)`; PINNED_COMPLAINTS entries have userId="0"/id="admin" and are never persisted; ComplaintViewModel.handleSubmitReply routes pinned parents through this path unconditionally.
suggestedFix: In replyToComplaint, fall back to constructing the LegacyComplaint from the ComplaintSummary (pre-#9 shape, using preserved summary fields + replyto) when the parent has status PINNED or when fetchLegacyById finds no row, instead of failing.
verifierNote: Verified: ComplaintActionRepositoryImpl.kt:98 replyToComplaint unconditionally calls fetchLegacyById (lines 129-131: getUser(userId).firstOrNull { it.id == id } ?: error(...)); pinned entries (userId="0", id="admin") are static in-binary values (PinnedComplaints.kt:92-124) never persisted to Firestore, so the re-fetch always fails -> Result.failure -> error snackbar. Reply IS offered on PINNED parents (ComplaintActionDialog.kt KDoc lines 106-108; ComplaintViewModel.handleSubmitReply:198-207 routes unconditionally). title: searchAllRepos has no per-repo catch: one throwing source kills the whole multi-source search
detail: The class KDoc (lines 52-55) promises "One repo failing yields an AppResult.Failure under its own api key — it does NOT sink the others (each repo's flow is independently catch-classified)", but no catch operator exists anywhere in searchAllRepos. A Throwable from `repo.initSite()`, `repo.getBaseUrl()` (the sequential warm-up loop at line 113 runs before any results at all), or a legacy `fetchSearchDataF` flow that throws instead of emitting State.Error (explicitly called out as common in MangaDetailsRepositoryImpl's KDoc: "many legacy sources throw on bad responses instead of emitting State.Error") propagates through merge() and cancels the entire fan-out. The collector (SearchViewModel.runMultiSearch) only has a terminal flow-level `.catch` that shows a generic error effect — every other source's section is left frozen on its `null` loading spinner with no terminal state. With ~50 scrapers subject to scraper rot, a single broken source realistically breaks aggregated search across all sources.

title: CBZ conversion cancelled mid-run leaves isConverting=true forever — undismissable stuck dialog on Settings re-entry

title: Unsynchronized mutable pagination state on a Koin single can be written back stale after a tab switch
detail: `accumulated` / `genericAccumulated` are plain `var`s on a singleton, mutated from coroutines on dispatchers.io. selectTab/selectSource clear them, but an in-flight fetchMore/fetchHome for the PREVIOUS source can complete after the clear (HomeViewModel cancels homeFetchJob, but the write-back in `.also { ... }` races the cancellation if the terminal network emission has already landed) and re-populate `accumulated` with the old source's items. The next fetchMore then hands the wrong `currentItems` snapshot to the new source's fetchMoreManga, which legacy sources append to — producing a mixed-source feed page. There is also no memory-visibility guarantee (no @Volatile/Mutex) between IO threads, though in practice the VM's serialized dispatch provides happens-before edges. The window is small but the consequence (cross-source feed bleed, exactly what the ManhastroDadosStore.clear() comment guards against) is user-visible.
evidence: Lines 86-89 plain `var accumulated` / `var genericAccumulated`; lines 105-117 clears in selectTab/selectSource; lines 141-143 and 171-177 write-backs in `.also` blocks that run after the suspend fetch completes.
suggestedFix: Guard the pagination state with a Mutex keyed to the fetch methods, or tag the accumulated snapshot with the source api and discard write-backs whose api no longer matches the active source.
verifierNote: HomeFeedRepositoryImpl.kt:86-89 plain vars on a Koin single; selectTab/selectSource clear at :105-117; write-backs run in non-suspending .also blocks after the suspend fetch (:134, :142, :161, :176), so Job.cancel cannot preempt a write-back whose terminal emission already landed - a stale old-source list can repopulate `accumulated` after the clear and feed the next source's fetchMoreManga (cross-source bleed). title: Inline-refresh re-entry guard is check-then-act: a rapid double refresh can double-run on Desktop/iOS
detail: refresh() checks `!inlineRefreshing.value` on the caller thread but only sets the flag to true INSIDE the launched coroutine on dispatchers.io. Two refresh() calls in quick succession (double pull-to-refresh, or pull + auto-refresh) can both pass the check before the first coroutine starts, launching two concurrent RefreshAllLibraryChaptersUseCase runs — the exact situation the comment says is guarded. Consequence is duplicated network fetches for every library manga (the Room inserts themselves are idempotent), plus the spinner flag being cleared by whichever run finishes first while the other is still running.
evidence: Lines 122-132: `else if (!inlineRefreshing.value) { scope.launch { inlineRefreshing.value = true; try { refreshAllChapters() } finally { inlineRefreshing.value = false } } }`.
suggestedFix: Use an atomic claim before launching, e.g. `if (!inlineRefreshing.compareAndSet(expect = false, update = true)) return` then launch with try/finally resetting to false.
verifierNote: LibraryRefreshRepositoryImpl.kt:122-133: refresh() checks !inlineRefreshing.value on the caller thread but sets the flag only inside the launched IO coroutine - two rapid calls both pass the check before the first coroutine runs (classic check-then-act). MutableStateFlow.compareAndSet exists in kotlinx.coroutines, so the suggested atomic claim compiles and preserves behavior except the double-run.

title: toFileUrl produces malformed file URLs for Windows paths and never percent-encodes
detail: `"file://$path"` assumes a Unix absolute path. On Windows Desktop (packageMsi is a supported distribution) the stored localImagePaths look like `C:\Users\...\chapter_5.cbz`, yielding `file://C:\Users\...` (authority = "C:", backslashes unescaped). Spaces or non-ASCII characters in the user-profile path are also passed through unencoded. Depending on Coil 3's lenient Uri parsing this may still resolve, but the downloaded-chapter offline read path silently falling back to network (or failing) on Windows is plausible.
evidence: Lines 203-204: `if (path.startsWith("file://")) path else "file://$path"`.
suggestedFix: Normalize via okio Path and build a proper URI (e.g. prefix with `file:///` and convert backslashes / encode segments), or pass the raw path to Coil (Coil 3 JVM resolves plain absolute paths via its file mapper).
verifierNote: ChapterPagesRepositoryImpl.kt:203-204: `"file://$path"` with no encoding; localPaths come from okio Path.toString() (backslashes on Windows JVM) so Windows Desktop (packageMsi is a documented distribution) yields `file://C:\...` with authority 'C:'. Whether Coil 3's lenient parser recovers is uncertain (hence medium confidence), but the malformed-URL claim is factually correct and the offline-read fallback consequence plausible.

title: replaceBaseUrl validates only the original URL — a blank/scheme-less server baseUrl permanently corrupts every stored URL for that source
detail: replaceBaseUrl guards `originalUrl` (no `://` -> returned unchanged) but never validates `newBaseUrl`. A remote source entry with a bumped baseVersion and a missing/empty/scheme-less `baseUrl` field (the manual parser defaults absent fields to "") rewrites every saved_manga/saved_chapters/history/notifications URL for that source to `"" + remainder` (host stripped) or `host-without-scheme + remainder` — and then bumps the persisted version so no later refresh repairs it. suggestedFix: At the top of replaceBaseUrl (or before calling propagateUrlChanges/updateBaseUrlAndVersionByName) add `if (!newBaseUrl.contains("://") || newBaseUrl.substringAfter("://").isBlank()) return originalUrl` / skip the upsert for that source.

title: KcefState.markInitialized() flips true even when KCEF.init failed via the onError callback
detail: KCEF (dev.datlag.kcef) delivers init failures to the onError callback and RETURNS NORMALLY (its internal state goes to Error, not Initialized) — that is the whole reason the suspend init() takes an onError callback at all. The code's comment at line 150 ('Reaching here means init returned without throwing -> KCEF is Initialized') is therefore wrong: when onError (line 140) or onRestartRequired (line 143) fires, execution still reaches KcefState.markInitialized() at line 153 and the process-wide initialized flag flips true on a FAILED init. This directly violates the file's own fail-safe contract KDoc (lines 61-65: 'On failure KcefState.initialized stays false and WebViewHost.desktop.kt renders its graceful placeholder/progress UI'). Practical impact today is bounded: WebViewHost.desktop.kt:97-115 re-checks via KCEF.newClientOrNullBlocking (returns null when KCEF state is not Initialized) and renders the terminal 'Embedded WebView unavailable' text instead of crashing — arguably even the better terminal UI than the infinite CircularProgressIndicator the documented contract would produce. But the flag is semantically wrong, and any future consumer of KcefState.initialized (or any UI distinguishing 'still initializing' from 'failed') will be misled.
evidence: runCatching { KCEF.init(builder = {...}, onError = { throwable -> throwable?.printStackTrace() }, onRestartRequired = {...}); KcefState.markInitialized() } — markInitialized() is unconditionally reached after init() returns, including the onError path.
suggestedFix: Track failure in the callbacks (e.g. `var initFailed = false; onError = { initFailed = true; it?.printStackTrace() }; onRestartRequired = { initFailed = true; ... }`) and only call KcefState.markInitialized() when !initFailed. Because WebViewHost shows an infinite spinner while initialized==false, pair this with a terminal failed state on KcefState (e.g. markFailed()) so the host can show the 'unavailable' placeholder instead of spinning forever — which is why this needs an owner/design decision rather than a one-line guard.
verifierNote: KCEF.init (dev.datlag.kcef 2025.03.23, verified from the jar: init(builder, InitError, InitRestartRequired) declares only throws KCEFException$Disposed) reports init failures via the onError callback and returns normally, so Main.kt:153 markInitialized() flips true on a failed init, contradicting the fail-safe KDoc (L61-65). Impact bounded as claimed: WebViewHost.desktop.kt:97-115 re-checks via newClientOrNullBlocking (null when state != Initialized) and shows the terminal 'unavailable' text. Risky is right — a bare guard would regress to the infinite spinner; needs a paired failed-state on KcefState.

title: SwingDispatcherFactory keep rule preserves only the class name, not the no-arg constructor ServiceLoader needs
detail: `-keep class kotlinx.coroutines.swing.SwingDispatcherFactory` (no member specification) tells ProGuard to keep the class as an entry point but does NOT keep its members — an unreferenced no-arg constructor can still be stripped by shrinking. kotlinx-coroutines resolves the main dispatcher factory via (Fast)ServiceLoader, which instantiates the class reflectively through its no-arg constructor; if the constructor is stripped, the Dispatchers.Swing lookup fails in exactly the packaged-release-only way this file's own header warns about ('a missing keep here would silently work in dev and only break in the packaged Msi/Dmg/Deb'). Note the org.cef rule above it correctly uses `{ *; }`. Library-shipped META-INF/proguard rules are an Android/R8 mechanism and are not auto-applied by the desktop ProGuard step, so this file is the only protection. Confidence is medium because the Compose Desktop plugin's bundled default rules may already keep coroutines service-loader internals on some plugin versions.
evidence: -keep class kotlinx.coroutines.swing.SwingDispatcherFactory   (no `{ ... }` member spec, unlike `-keep class org.cef.** { *; }` at line 16)
suggestedFix: Change line 21 to: -keep class kotlinx.coroutines.swing.SwingDispatcherFactory { *; }   (or at minimum `{ <init>(); }`).
verifierNote: ProGuard semantics correct: '-keep class X' without a member spec keeps the class name but not its members, so the reflectively-invoked no-arg <init>() of the ServiceLoader-instantiated SwingDispatcherFactory can be shrunk away; release shrinking is wired (desktopApp/build.gradle.kts buildTypes.release.proguard -> compose-desktop.pro), and the org.cef rule on L16 correctly uses { *; }. Medium-confidence hedge re plugin default rules stands; the { *; } fix is harmless either way.

title: markAsRead() implements a TOGGLE, violating the :domain UpdatesRepository.markAsRead contract ('re-emits with isRead = true')
detail: UpdatesRepositoryImpl.markAsRead forwards to LibraryDeo.markChapterAndNotificationRead(entry.chapterId), whose @Transaction body runs `UPDATE saved_chapters SET isRead = NOT isRead` + `UPDATE notifications SET isRead = NOT isRead` (LibraryDeo.kt:99-108) — i.e. it FLIPS the read flags rather than setting them. The :domain interface KDoc (UpdatesRepository.kt:87-89) promises 'the upstream observeUpdates flow re-emits with the entry's isRead = true', so calling markAsRead (or MarkUpdateAsReadUseCase, which is unguarded) on an already-read entry silently un-reads it AND flips the underlying saved chapter's read flag. Today this is masked only because the single caller, UpdatesViewModel, guards with `!entry.isRead` — a guard its own KDoc calls 'load-bearing: the DAO query is a toggle... re-marking a read row would flip it back to unread'. The non-idempotent semantic is a landmine for any future caller and contradicts the published domain contract; the impl's own KDoc (lines 62-70) documents the NOT-toggle accurately, so the mismatch is between the :data behavior and the :domain promise.
evidence: Impl: `libraryDeo.markChapterAndNotificationRead(entry.chapterId)` -> DAO: `@Query("UPDATE notifications SET isRead = NOT isRead WHERE chapterId = :chapterId")`. Domain contract: 'the upstream [observeUpdates] flow re-emits with the entry's isRead = true once the Room transaction commits.' VM guard KDoc: 'The !isRead guard is load-bearing'.
suggestedFix: Make the impl honor the contract by short-circuiting already-read entries: `override suspend fun markAsRead(entry: UpdateEntry) { if (!entry.isRead) libraryDeo.markChapterAndNotificationRead(entry.chapterId) }` (keeps the shared/parity DAO untouched), or alternatively re-document UpdatesRepository.markAsRead + MarkUpdateAsReadUseCase as a toggle. Owner should choose; the DAO itself is legacy-shared and must not change.
verifierNote: Verified end-to-end: LibraryDeo.kt:99-108 runs `SET isRead = NOT isRead` on both tables (a toggle); UpdatesRepositoryImpl.markAsRead (:144) forwards unconditionally; the :domain contract (UpdatesRepository.kt:87-89) promises 're-emits with isRead = true'; MarkUpdateAsReadUseCase is unguarded and only UpdatesViewModel's '!entry.isRead' guard (:215, self-described as load-bearing) masks the non-idempotence. Contract/impl mismatch confirmed; DAO is legacy-shared parity so the short-circuit-in-impl vs re-document choice is the owner's -> risky.

title: Admin-wide complaint read (all users' submissions incl. userIds) is gated only by a client-side navigation check
detail: loadAllComplaints returns every complaint in the Firestore collection, including other users' userIds and device metadata. Per the method KDoc (lines 172-176), 'this repository doesn't gate on identity - gating happens at navigation time' via the client-side Admin.isAdmin check in the route adapter. Client-side gating is trivially bypassable (modified client / direct Firestore SDK calls with the app's config); the only real protection is the Firestore security rules, which are not visible in this repo and cannot be verified from the client. If the rules allow any authenticated/anonymous app identity to read the complaints collection (which the working user-side path suggests is at least partially true), every user's complaint history and userId is exposed. This mirrors the native design (parity), so it is reported for owner verification of the Firestore rules rather than as a client code fix.
evidence: L172-176: 'The current admin-status check lives in the route adapter ... this repository doesn't gate on identity - gating happens at navigation time, not data-access time.' APP_MAP risk profile: 'admin actions; Firestore rules unseen from client'.
suggestedFix: Verify the Firestore security rules restrict collection-wide reads (and admin mutations: status change, closure reason, delete, edit) to authenticated admin identities server-side; if they do not, enforce it in rules - client-side Admin.isAdmin must not be the only gate.
verifierNote: KDoc L172-175 confirms identity gating happens only at navigation time via client-side Admin.isAdmin; Firestore rules are not in the repo so server-side enforcement is unverifiable from code. Matches the APP_MAP risk profile ('admin actions; Firestore rules unseen from client'); parity-with-native noted but potential exposure of all users' complaint data + userIds justifies the report-only owner-verification ask.

title: clear(url) has zero callers — the documented pruning hook for the process-singleton progress map is never exercised, so the map only ever grows
detail: The interface's own lifecycle section (lines 47-51) warns that the Koin-`single` impl's map 'grows monotonically per process' and that pruning is 'driven by an explicit caller — see [clear]', and the member KDoc says the Reader VM MAY call clear in onCleared 'to keep the in-memory map from growing without bound across long sessions'. Repo-wide grep shows no caller of clear(url) anywhere: only `report` (via ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute's `pageProgressRepo::report` feeding the OkHttp/Ktor interceptors and the Coil listener) and `observe` (via ObservePageProgressUseCase) are used. Because the shared image client wraps EVERY image response (covers + pages, per KtorPageProgressObserver's 'why every response is wrapped' note), every image URL ever loaded leaves a permanent entry in the singleton map for the process lifetime. Practically this is a slow, bounded-by-usage leak (string keys + small status objects), but it means the declared cleanup contract is dead code and the documented mitigation never happens.
evidence: grep for `.clear(` across core/domain/data/platform/presentation/ui/composeApp/app/shared finds no PageProgressRepository.clear call; only `readProgress.clear(it)` (a different repository) appears. Route adapter uses only `pageProgressRepo::report` (ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute.kt:163).
suggestedFix: Either wire clearing into the Reader teardown (e.g. ReaderViewModel clears the previous chapter's page URLs on chapter switch / onCleared, via a small ClearPageProgressUseCase) or remove clear() from the interface and impl and update the lifecycle KDoc to state the map intentionally accumulates per process.

title: runCatching swallows CancellationException in the Download-all orchestration
detail: invoke() wraps the whole withContext(dispatchers.io) resolve+enqueue loop in runCatching. If the Details VM scope is cancelled mid-loop (user navigates away during a long 'Download all' over hundreds of chapters), withContext throws CancellationException and runCatching captures it, returning Result.failure(CancellationException) instead of letting cancellation propagate. This violates the repo-wide contract (CLAUDE.md / contract section 9-10: 'CancellationException is always re-thrown') and misreports cooperative cancellation as an operation failure to the caller. Every other error-classifying site in the rework (e.g. HomeFeedRepositoryImpl.activeRepoResult, lines 222-228) explicitly rethrows CancellationException before classifying; this is the one rework orchestration that does not.
evidence: suspend operator fun invoke(details: MangaDetails): Result<Unit> = runCatching { withContext(dispatchers.io) { details.chapters.forEach { ... } } }  — no CancellationException rethrow; contrast with data/repository/HomeFeedRepositoryImpl.kt L224-225 'catch (ce: CancellationException) { throw ce }'.
suggestedFix: Replace runCatching with an explicit try/catch that rethrows CancellationException: try { withContext(dispatchers.io) { ... }; Result.success(Unit) } catch (ce: CancellationException) { throw ce } catch (t: Throwable) { Result.failure(t) }.
verifierNote: Claim is factually correct (stdlib runCatching at EnqueueAllChaptersDownloadUseCase.kt:61 captures CE; the project ships core/util/runCatchingCancellable.kt expressly to avoid this), but downgraded to minor: zero user-visible effect today — the caller's failure branch is statically dead (see code-ak-2) and the coroutine is already cancelled, so propagating vs swallowing produces identical observable behavior. Pure contract-hygiene fix (swap in runCatchingCancellable, :domain already depends on :core).

title: Download-all failures can never reach the user: Result carries raw Throwable but the sole caller only surfaces AppError
detail: The KDoc ('Result semantics', L36-41) promises 'The caller surfaces a failure via the existing error snackbar effect'. That is unfulfillable: kotlin.Result.failure can only carry a Throwable, and AppError (core/error/AppError.kt L81, 'sealed class AppError') does NOT extend Throwable — so the failure payload is always a raw exception (e.g. a Room/SQLite throw out of ChapterIdResolverImpl). The only caller, DetailsViewModel.onDownloadAllClick (presentation/.../details/DetailsViewModel.kt L678-679), guards the snackbar with 'onFailure { error -> if (error is AppError) emit(DetailsEffect.ShowError(error)) }' — a check that can never be true. Net effect: any orchestration failure of 'Download all' (a core download flow) is silently dropped; the user taps the button, nothing happens, no feedback. The use case's own KDoc claim is therefore also stale/incorrect.
evidence: Use case returns Result<Unit> built by runCatching (raw Throwable payloads only, since Result.failure requires Throwable and AppError is not a Throwable); DetailsViewModel.kt L679: '.onFailure { error -> if (error is AppError) emit(DetailsEffect.ShowError(error)) }' — statically impossible match, so the error snackbar branch is dead.
suggestedFix: Either (a) change the use case to return AppResult<Unit>, classifying caught throwables to AppError (e.g. AppError.Unexpected(cause = t)) like the home/details fetch use cases, and have DetailsViewModel emit ShowError unconditionally on Failure; or (b) keep Result and have DetailsViewModel map any failure to AppError.Unexpected before emitting ShowError. Option (b) is the smallest diff but the AppResult signature matches the rework boundary convention. Needs owner decision on signature; coordinate with the DetailsViewModel shard (duplicate manifestation).
verifierNote: Verified empirically: AppError.kt:81 'sealed class AppError' has no Throwable supertype, and a scratch compile in :core proved 'Throwable is AppError' compiles silently yet can never be true — DetailsViewModel.kt:679's 'if (error is AppError) emit(ShowError)' is statically dead, so any orchestration throw (e.g. Room error in ChapterIdResolverImpl; EnqueueDownloadUseCase absorbs its own failures into an ignored Result) is silently dropped with no user feedback. KDoc promise at the use case L36-41 unfulfillable. Signature decision needed, fixSafety risky stands.

title: Untyped suspend boundary: a throw from active-repo resolution escapes raw instead of returning a typed result

The impl (data/repository/HomeFeedRepositoryImpl.kt L204-210) resolves the active source via the unprotected activeRepo() — the same impl added activeRepoResult() (L222-228) precisely because that resolution can throw (e.g. a Room read error in the active-repo flow). title: Download-all is an N+1 loop: one url->id Room query plus one entity re-load per chapter
detail: For a manga with N chapters, the loop issues N sequential ChapterDao.getChapterIdByUrl queries (ChapterIdResolverImpl), and each enqueueDownload then re-loads the matching SavedChapterEntity by id in the :data impl — roughly 2N round-trips through Room plus N legacy enqueue calls, executed sequentially. For long series (1000+ chapters on the scraped sources) this delays the queue becoming visible on the Downloads screen. It runs on dispatchers.io so the UI thread is unaffected, hence minor. A single bulk query (resolve all ids for the manga, or load saved chapters by mangaId) would collapse the per-chapter resolution.
evidence: details.chapters.forEach { chapter -> val chapterId = chapterIdResolver.resolveChapterId(chapter.url) ?: return@forEach; enqueueDownload(chapterId = chapterId, ...) } — per-chapter suspend Room query inside the loop.
suggestedFix: Add a bulk resolver port (e.g. suspend fun resolveChapterIds(urls: List<String>): Map<String, Long>) backed by a single 'WHERE url IN (...)' DAO query (chunked to stay under SQLite's 999-variable limit), then loop over the resolved map. Keep per-chapter enqueue semantics unchanged.
verifierNote: N+1 structure confirmed: L63-69 issues one resolveChapterId Room query per chapter sequentially, and enqueueDownload re-loads the SavedChapterEntity by id in the impl (interface KDoc L129-133) — ~2N sequential round-trips for download-all. Adjusted on impact wording: rows appear on the Downloads screen incrementally as each enqueue lands (Room flow re-emits per write), so visibility is gradual rather than blocked; the tail of a 1000+-chapter queue is what arrives late. Severity/fixSafety unchanged.
