Native MangaViewModel.kt:169 has initSite only in startHomeFetch.
suggestedFix: Correct the KDoc to state that only fetchHome performs initSite() (native parity) and that fetchMore/fetchFeatured rely on the home fetch / BaseManga-internal ensureSiteInitialized for header hydration.
verifierNote: KDoc lines 53-55 ('each preceded by initSite() + getBaseUrl()') contradicts the code: fetchHome (139-140) calls initSite+getBaseUrl, fetchMore (170) calls neither, fetchFeatured (190) calls getBaseUrl only. Native parity sub-claim verified: native MangaViewModel.kt:169 is the sole initSite call (startHomeFetch only). Stale-KDoc-contradicting-code is an explicit minor finding category per APP_MAP; doc-only fix.

title: Desktop singleton HttpClient installs HttpCache with default unlimited in-memory storage (unfixed twin of the known Android finding)
detail: The known finding for HttpClientFactory.android.kt:70 (install(HttpCache) with default unlimited in-memory storage on the singleton client that downloads chapter images) has an identical, unreported twin in the Desktop factory. SharedModule.kt:118 binds this client as the process singleton, and on Desktop the download engine (shared/src/nonAndroidMain/.../clean/CoroutineDownloadRepositoryImpl.kt:386,401) downloads every chapter page through it via httpClient.get(imageUrl) + response.body<ByteArray>(). Ktor's default HttpCache storage is an unbounded in-memory CacheStorage, so every cacheable response body — including multi-MB manga page images served with long max-age headers (the in-file comment even cites manhastro's 1-day Cache-Control window as the motivation) — is retained in process memory for the app's lifetime. A bulk chapter download grows heap without bound; there is no eviction.
evidence: HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt:41-43: '// Enables cross-request response caching so Cache-Control directives (incl. the 1-day window for manhastro /dados) are honored ... install(HttpCache)'. Consumer: CoroutineDownloadRepositoryImpl.downloadOnePage() 'val bytes: ByteArray = response.body()' on the same Koin singleton client.
suggestedFix: Apply whatever remediation is chosen for the Android twin to all three factories: either drop HttpCache from the image-downloading client, bound it (publicStorage(FileStorage(cacheDir))) so cached bodies live on disk with finite scope, or route chapter-image downloads through a cache-free client. Fix must land in HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt and HttpClientFactory.ios.kt together with the already-flagged android file.
verifierNote: HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt:43 installs HttpCache with no storage config (Ktor default = unbounded in-memory CacheStorage); SharedModule.kt:118 binds it single; PlatformModule.desktop.kt:157-160 wires the same shared client into CoroutineDownloadRepositoryImpl, whose downloadOnePage (lines 386-401) GETs every chapter page and materialises body<ByteArray>() — cacheable multi-MB image bodies accumulate for process lifetime with no eviction. Per-file twin of the known Android finding (separate file, separate edit — not an in-batch duplicate).

title: iOS singleton HttpClient installs HttpCache with default unlimited in-memory storage (unfixed twin of the known Android finding)
detail: Same defect class as the known HttpClientFactory.android.kt:70 finding and r2-res-1, in the iOS factory. The iOS download pipeline (CoroutineDownloadRepositoryImpl in nonAndroidMain) pulls every chapter page through this singleton Darwin client, and Ktor's default HttpCache keeps every cacheable response body in an unbounded in-memory store. iOS is the worst-hit platform: there is no SD-card-sized heap headroom — jetsam terminates the app under memory pressure, so a long downloading session can be killed mid-download by the cache itself. The body bytes are additionally fully materialised per page (response.body<ByteArray>()), so peak memory is cache + in-flight page.
evidence: HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:40-42: '// Enables cross-request response caching ... install(HttpCache)' on the client bound single { createHttpClient() } in SharedModule.kt:118.
suggestedFix: Same as r2-res-1: bound/disk-backed cache storage or remove HttpCache from the client used for image downloads; fix the three per-platform factories together.
verifierNote: HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:42 identical install(HttpCache) with default unbounded in-memory storage; PlatformModule.ios.kt:174-185 binds CoroutineDownloadRepositoryImpl with httpClient = get() (the SharedModule.kt:118 singleton), so the iOS download pipeline pulls every page through it. Jetsam-kill-under-memory-pressure escalation is plausible on iOS. Per-file twin of r2-res-1/the Android finding; kept separate because each platform factory needs its own edit.

title: Notification cover fetch never closes the InputStream / disconnects the URLConnection
detail: showChapterNotification fetches the manga cover with BitmapFactory.decodeStream(url.openConnection().getInputStream()) and never closes the stream nor disconnects the HttpURLConnection. The existing known finding on this line covers missing timeouts/headers only; the resource leak is distinct: each notification with a cover leaks an open stream + pooled connection until finalization. addChapterNotification fires up to 6 notifications per manga per library refresh (pairs.takeLast(6)), so a refresh across a large library leaks dozens of FDs in a burst. decodeStream also returns null on failure here, but the connection is still left open in that path.
evidence: Line 129-134: 'val bitmap = async(Dispatchers.IO) { runCatching { val url = URL(notification.mangaImageUrl); BitmapFactory.decodeStream(url.openConnection().getInputStream()) }.getOrNull() }.await()' — no .use{}, no disconnect().
suggestedFix: Open the connection into a local, wrap getInputStream() in .use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it) }, and call connection.disconnect() in a finally block (combine with the already-flagged timeout fix).
verifierNote: ChapterNotificationHelper.kt:129-134: BitmapFactory.decodeStream(url.openConnection().getInputStream()) with no .use{} and no disconnect() — decodeStream does not close the stream, and the connection stays open on both success and null-decode paths. Burst factor verified: pairs.takeLast(6) per manga per refresh (line 118). Distinct from the known timeout finding on the same lines as claimed.

title: Skia Image/Data from page-share PNG encode are never closed (Desktop + iOS twins) — native memory held until GC finalizer
detail: encodeImageBitmapToPng builds Image.makeFromBitmap(bitmap.asSkiaBitmap()) — a full native-memory copy of the shared reader page (manga pages are tall; tens of MB at full resolution) — then encodeToData(PNG), and closes neither the Image nor the Data. Both are skiko Managed objects whose native memory is reclaimed only when the Cleaner runs after JVM/K-N GC, so each share action leaves a multi-MB native allocation pending for an unbounded time, on top of the synchronous main-thread encode already flagged for the call site. The identical code ships in ImageBitmapPngEncoder.ios.kt:19. This contradicts the module's own discipline: SkiaWebpEncoder.kt closes image/bandImage/bitmap explicitly, and the failure to close a Skia bitmap on one path of HighQualitySkiaImageDecoder is already an accepted finding.
evidence: runCatching { Image.makeFromBitmap(bitmap.asSkiaBitmap()).encodeToData(EncodedImageFormat.PNG)?.bytes }.getOrNull() — no use{}/close() on the Image or the returned Data; same body byte-for-byte in the iOS actual.
suggestedFix: In both actuals: val image = Image.makeFromBitmap(...); try { image.encodeToData(PNG)?.use { it.bytes } } finally { image.close() } (okio-style use is available on skiko Data via Closeable; otherwise close in finally).
verifierNote: Both actuals byte-identical (ImageBitmapPngEncoder.desktop.kt:18-22, ImageBitmapPngEncoder.ios.kt:18-22): neither the skiko Image from makeFromBitmap nor the returned Data is closed — both are Managed natives reclaimed only by the GC-driven Cleaner, so each share leaves multi-MB native allocations pending. Discipline contrast verified: SkiaWebpEncoder.kt closes image/bandImage/bitmap explicitly (lines 73/101/104). Suggested use{}/close-in-finally fix compiles (Managed is AutoCloseable).

title: Raw Firestore HTTP response body is embedded in the thrown exception message and surfaced verbatim to the user snackbar (info disclosure + i18n leak)
detail: sendComplaint (L86), updateComplaint (L153) and deleteComplaint (L166) all build the failure exception as error("Firestore <verb> failed: HTTP ${response.status.value}: $raw"), where $raw = response.bodyAsText() — the full Firestore REST error payload. This is the iOS/Desktop complaint backend (commonMain, used on every non-Android target). On the user-side complaint flow, ComplaintViewModel.completeAction (presentation/.../complaint/ComplaintViewModel.kt:243) takes result.exceptionOrNull()?.message and emits it straight to the UI via ComplaintEffect.ShowErrorMessage(message); the admin flow does the same. So a failed reply/edit/delete (e.g. a 403 from Firestore rules, or any 4xx/5xx) shows the raw Firestore JSON error body — which can include the GCP project id, database path, and rule-evaluation diagnostics — directly in a user-facing snackbar, untranslated, in all 10 locales. This is distinct from the already-known systemic 'effects carry hardcoded English copy' finding (presentation layer) and the known 'client-side-only admin gating' finding: the new issue is the data source deliberately concatenating the untrusted server response body into the exception text that propagates to end users. The Android Firebase-SDK sibling (ComplaintFirestoreDataSource) does not stringify a raw HTTP body this way, so the leak is REST-target-specific.
evidence: L84-86: val raw = response.bodyAsText(); log.e {...}; error("Firestore create failed: HTTP ${response.status.value}: $raw")  +  ComplaintViewModel.kt:242-247 val message = result.exceptionOrNull()?.let { e -> e.message ?: e::class.simpleName } ?: "Unknown error"; emit(ComplaintEffect.ShowErrorMessage(message))
suggestedFix: Do not concatenate $raw into the exception message that reaches the UI. Keep the raw body only in the log.e line (already present), and throw a stable, non-leaking message such as error("Firestore <verb> failed: HTTP ${response.status.value}"). Better, map the failure to a typed AppError at the :data boundary so :ui renders a localized string instead of the throwable message.
verifierNote: Chain verified: ComplaintFirestoreRestDataSource.kt:84-86/150-154/163-167 concatenate the full Firestore response body into error(...), and ComplaintViewModel.completeAction (lines 242-248) emits exceptionOrNull()?.message verbatim to the user snackbar. Two corrections: fixSafety report-only was wrong — the file is shared/** but NOT sources_repositry/** (only that subtree is report-only), and the log-only/stable-message fix is contained → safe. Severity downgraded to minor: project id/database path are already in the client's COLLECTION_URL constant, so the novel disclosure (rule diagnostics) is mild; the real harm is raw untranslated JSON in the error snackbar — hygiene, not a security boundary breach.

title: Host-move URL propagation rewrites saved_manga.url via @Update(onConflict=REPLACE) — a unique-url collision silently deletes another library row (and its chapters/downloads)
detail: updateMangaUrls() (and the upsert path that calls it on every baseVersion bump) rewrites each stored manga URL with mangaDao.updateManga(manga.copy(url = newUrl)). MangaDao.updateManga is declared @Update(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE) and saved_manga has a UNIQUE index on url, so if the rewritten URL collides with a different saved_manga row's url (e.g. the same manga was saved once under the old host and once under the new host across a host move, or a previous propagation was partially applied), SQLite's REPLACE conflict resolution DELETES the pre-existing conflicting row before applying the update. With the FK pragma on, the v10 CASCADE FKs then wipe that row's saved_chapters and chapter_downloads (read flags, bookmarks, download bookkeeping); with the pragma off (the known multi-connection pragma gap) they become permanent orphans. The native parity source did NOT have this hazard: native's updateMangaUrls calls the bare `mangaDao.update(updatedManga)` (default ABORT), so a collision merely throws and is caught/logged, preserving both rows. The KMP port lost the bare update() during DAO pruning and substituted the REPLACE variant, silently widening a logged no-op into row deletion. The image-URL pass (line 231) is unaffected (imageUrl has no unique index).
evidence: SourceRegistryRefreshRepositoryImpl.kt:194 `if (newUrl != manga.url) mangaDao.updateManga(manga.copy(url = newUrl))`; MangaDao.kt:78-79 `@Update(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE) suspend fun updateManga(...)`; SavedMangaEntity.kt:17 `indices = [Index(value = ["url"], unique = true)]`; native-app MangaDao.kt:120-121 has the bare `@Update suspend fun update(manga: SavedMangaEntity)` which native's UpdateSourcesRepository.updateMangaUrls uses (`mangaDao.update(updatedManga)`).
suggestedFix: Add a bare `@Update suspend fun update(manga: SavedMangaEntity)` (default ABORT conflict) to MangaDao — mirroring native — and use it in updateMangaUrls()/updateMangaImageUrls() so a url collision aborts that single row rewrite (already caught by perTable) instead of deleting the colliding library row.
verifierNote: All four evidence legs verified: MangaDao.kt:78-79 is @Update(onConflict=REPLACE), SavedMangaEntity.kt:17 has unique url index, SavedChapterEntity/ChapterDownloadEntity carry onDelete=CASCADE FKs, and native MangaDao.kt:116 is a bare @Update used by native UpdateSourcesRepository.kt:286 — so the KMP port (SourceRegistryRefreshRepositoryImpl.kt:194) did widen a logged abort into silent row deletion + cascade. Data loss is real but gated on the old-host/new-host duplicate-row collision pre-state, so major (not critical) is calibrated right.

title: groupByDate drops notifications dated exactly 7 days ago (and future-dated rows) from observeUpdates — they vanish from the Updates screen for a day
detail: groupByDate buckets rows with strict comparisons: lastWeekList takes `> lastWeek && < yesterday`, olderList takes `< lastWeek`. A notification whose notificationDate equals exactly today-7d matches NO bucket (not == today/yesterday, not > lastWeek, not < lastWeek), and any future-dated row (device clock skew, timezone change) also matches no bucket. Because observeUpdates() flattens the buckets (`flatMap { (_, entries) -> entries }`), these rows are silently dropped from the emitted list — the entry disappears from the Updates screen on day 7 and reappears the next day as 'Older'; while invisible it cannot be marked read or deleted. The strict comparisons are a verbatim port of native's groupByDate (isAfter/isBefore), so this is native parity — but it is a harmful invariant (a row in the table that the screen cannot show), which the ground rules say to note.
evidence: UpdatesRepositoryImpl.kt:192-195 `.filter { it.notificationDate > lastWeek && it.notificationDate < yesterday }` / `.filter { it.notificationDate < lastWeek }` with `lastWeek = today.minus(DatePeriod(days = 7))`; line 140 flattens the buckets, so unbucketed rows never reach the UI.
suggestedFix: Make olderList the complement bucket (e.g. `filter { it.notificationDate <= lastWeek }` plus clamp future dates into todayList, or build olderList as `notifications - todayList - yesterdayList - lastWeekList`) so every row lands in exactly one bucket.
verifierNote: Hole confirmed: UpdatesRepositoryImpl.kt:190-195 buckets leave date==today-7d and future dates unmatched, and observeUpdates (line 140) flattens buckets so those rows vanish for a day. But it is a verbatim port of native NotificationRepository.kt:55-60 (isAfter/isBefore, same strict bounds) — the suggested fix deviates from native bucketing, so fixSafety downgraded safe→risky (parity-affecting behavior change needs owner sign-off).

title: persistNewChaptersAndNotify resolves each new chapter id with a per-chapter url-only query, outside any transaction
detail: After inserting the new chapters in one batch, the notify pass runs `chapterDao.getChapterIdByUrl(ch.url)` once per new chapter (N+1 suspend DAO calls during a library refresh that can discover dozens of chapters across many manga). Two data-integrity wrinkles: (1) the lookup is by url alone with LIMIT 1, but the saved_chapters unique index is (mangaId, url) — the same chapter url saved under a DIFFERENT manga (legal duplicate across manga from the same source) can win the LIMIT 1, attaching the notification's chapterId to the wrong manga's chapter row, which later makes LibraryDeo.markChapterAndNotificationRead flip the wrong chapter's isRead; (2) the chapter insert (inside insertNewChapters) and the notification insert are separate writes with no shared transaction — a crash between them permanently loses the Updates entries for chapters that were persisted.
evidence: LibraryRepositoryImpl.kt:196-210 `newOnes.mapNotNull { ch -> val chapterId = chapterDao.getChapterIdByUrl(ch.url) ?: return@mapNotNull null ... }` after `insertNewChapters(...)`; ChapterDao.kt:106-107 `SELECT id FROM saved_chapters WHERE url = :url LIMIT 1`; SavedChapterEntity unique index is (mangaId, url).
suggestedFix: Resolve ids in one query scoped by mangaId (e.g. `SELECT id, url FROM saved_chapters WHERE mangaId = :mangaId AND url IN (:urls)`), build the notifications from that map, and wrap insert-chapters + insert-notifications in a single @Transaction DAO method.
verifierNote: Facts verified (LibraryRepositoryImpl.kt:196-209 N+1 getChapterIdByUrl, ChapterDao.kt:106-107 url-only LIMIT 1 vs (mangaId,url) unique index at SavedChapterEntity.kt:31, separate non-transactional notification insert) — but the narrative omits that this is native parity: native ChapterNotificationHelper.kt:84 resolves ids with the identical url-only ChapterDao.getChapterIdByUrl (native ChapterDao.kt:47-48). Parity-origin hazard, not a KMP regression; wrong-manga LIMIT 1 hit is also speculative in real data. Minor stands.

title: deleteDownloadedChapters — the only correct full-cleanup path for downloaded chapters (clear isDownloaded + delete files) — has zero callers
detail: deleteDownloadedChapters(chapters) is the one routine that performs the consistent two-store cleanup: chapterDao.markChaptersNotDownloaded(ids) (clears saved_chapters.isDownloaded + localImagePaths) plus fileService.deleteChapterFiles per chapter. A repo-wide grep finds no production call site — its only mention is a comment in DownloadsActionRepositoryImpl pointing at it as 'the SEPARATE Library delete-downloaded path'. The live delete affordances instead use either row-only deleteDownload (chapter_downloads row only; files + isDownloaded left behind — the known DetailsViewModel finding) or ChapterDeletionRepositoryImpl.deleteChapter (saved_chapters row only; on-disk files AND the chapter_downloads SUCCESS row both survive, so the Downloads screen keeps listing a chapter whose library row is gone). The cross-store invariant 'isDownloaded flag == files on disk == chapter_downloads SUCCESS row' currently has no code path that maintains it on deletion; the routine that would is dead.
evidence: grep for `deleteDownloadedChapters` across the repo returns only the definition (LibraryRepository.kt:184) and a comment reference in DownloadsActionRepositoryImpl.kt:175; ChapterDeletionRepositoryImpl.deleteChapter only calls chapterDao.deleteChapterById.
suggestedFix: Owner decision: either wire deleteDownloadedChapters (or a rework equivalent that also removes the chapter_downloads row) into the Details/Downloads delete flows, or delete the dead method once the rework grows its own consistent cleanup path.
verifierNote: Repo-wide grep matches the claim exactly: only the definition (shared LibraryRepository.kt:184) and a comment pointer in DownloadsActionRepositoryImpl.kt:175; ChapterDeletionRepositoryImpl.kt:14 is a bare deleteChapterById with no file/download-row cleanup. Dead consistent-cleanup path confirmed; wiring it in is an owner decision, so risky is right.

title: Seven Details download/cancel/delete action failures can never reach the user: `if (error is AppError)` is always false on kotlin.Result failures
detail: All per-chapter and bulk download-management actions in DetailsViewModel surface failures with the pattern `.onFailure { error -> if (error is AppError) emit(DetailsEffect.ShowError(error)) }` on a kotlin.Result<Unit>. The lambda parameter is Throwable, and AppError (core/.../AppError.kt:81) is a plain sealed class that does NOT extend Throwable — so the `is AppError` check is statically always false. The backing DownloadsActionRepositoryImpl wraps every mutation in runCatchingCancellable and produces raw Throwables (e.g. IllegalStateException("chapter row not found"), Room write failures, worker-enqueue rejections), never AppError. Affected user actions, each silently no-oping on failure with zero feedback: single-chapter download enqueue (line 801), per-chapter cancel incl. running-download interrupt (823), multi-select download (882), multi-select delete-downloads (915), per-row delete-chapter download cleanup (935), top-bar delete-all-downloads (976), top-bar cancel-all-downloads (993). A user who taps Download on a chapter whose enqueue fails sees nothing — no snackbar, no state change, no retry hint. The known finding on EnqueueAllChaptersDownloadUseCase.kt:36 covers only the download-all call site (line 679); these seven other paths through different use cases were missed.
evidence: DetailsViewModel.kt:801 `.onFailure { error -> if (error is AppError) emit(DetailsEffect.ShowError(error)) }` (same pattern at 823/882/915/935/976/993); AppError.kt:81 `sealed class AppError { abstract val cause: Throwable? ... }` (not a Throwable subtype); DownloadsActionRepositoryImpl.kt:139-195 wraps all mutations in runCatchingCancellable producing raw Throwables only.
suggestedFix: Replace the dead type-check with an unconditional mapping, e.g. `.onFailure { t -> emit(DetailsEffect.ShowError(AppError.Unexpected(message = t.message ?: "action failed", cause = t))) }` at all seven sites (or convert DownloadsActionRepository to return AppResult<Unit> per contract §9/§10, which the existing kotlin.Result-port finding already proposes).
verifierNote: AppError.kt:81 is a plain sealed class (not Throwable), and Kotlin single class inheritance makes `error is AppError` on a kotlin.Result<Unit> Throwable statically always-false; DownloadsActionRepository returns Result<Unit> via runCatchingCancellable raw Throwables (impl lines 139-195). All seven cited sites verified at DetailsViewModel.kt 801/823/882/915/935/976/993; line 679 is the separately-known sibling. Seven silent-failure user actions = major.

title: Retry on a failed genre/sort browse dispatches OnSubmit, which clears the error and searches nothing — error pane silently replaced by a blank idle screen
detail: The single-source error pane wires `onRetry = { onIntent(SearchIntent.OnSubmit) }`. A genre-chip browse runs with a blanked query (`runSingleSearch(query = "", modeOverride = GENRES)` — native parity), and a sort browse passes whatever `state.query` holds (often blank). When such a search fails, the pane shows Retry — but OnSubmit routes through `runSearch(state.query, ...)`, whose blank-query guard (SearchViewModel.kt:156-159) resets `single = UiState.Success(emptyList())` and returns without searching. Net effect of tapping Retry after a failed genre/sort browse with a blank text query: the error and retry affordance vanish, the genre search is NOT re-run, and because `isIdle = state.query.isBlank()` the screen renders the pristine idle state — indistinguishable from 'search worked, no results yet'. Even with a non-blank query, OnSubmit forces `singleModeOverride = SearchMode.NORMAL`, so the retried search is a different (normal) search rather than the failed genre/sort browse. Distinct from the known OnApplyFilters finding (SearchIntent.kt:32, a dead intent): this is the live error-pane retry path.
evidence: SearchScreen.kt:242 `onRetry = { onIntent(SearchIntent.OnSubmit) }`; SearchViewModel.kt:98-103 onSubmit → runSearch(query, mode, singleModeOverride = NORMAL); SearchViewModel.kt:156-159 `if (query.isBlank()) { updateState { it.copy(single = UiState.Success(emptyList()), multi = emptyMap()) }; return }`; SearchViewModel.kt:124-135 onGenreClick fires the browse with query="".
suggestedFix: Make retry re-run the failed search: record the last-executed single-search parameters (query + effective SearchMode + sort/genres) in the VM and add a SearchIntent.OnRetrySingle handled by re-invoking runSingleSearch with them; wire the error pane's onRetry to that intent instead of OnSubmit.
verifierNote: Traced end-to-end: SearchScreen.kt:242 onRetry→OnSubmit; SearchViewModel.kt:102 forces singleModeOverride=NORMAL; runSearch blank-guard at 156-159 clears the error to Success(emptyList()) and returns without searching; onGenreClick (line 133) browses with query="" so a failed genre browse's Retry lands exactly in that guard and renders the pristine idle screen (isIdle = query.isBlank(), SearchScreen.kt:235). Live error-pane path, distinct from the dead OnApplyFilters intent.

title: Desktop/iOS inline library refresh discards the AppResult — pull-to-refresh failure is indistinguishable from 'no new chapters'
detail: On Desktop/iOS the pull-to-refresh runs RefreshAllLibraryChaptersUseCase inline, but its AppResult<Int> return value is dropped on the floor (`refreshAllChapters()` inside launch, result unused). A total refresh failure (AppResult.Failure from a thrown library read) and the new-chapter count both vanish: the spinner stops (finally block) and the user gets no error, no count, no retry hint — stale data presented as a successful refresh. Compounding it, the use case's refreshOne collapses every per-manga fetch failure to 0 (RefreshAllLibraryChaptersUseCase.kt:72), so even 'every source failed' surfaces as Success(0) — a fully-failed refresh over existing content is silently identical to 'library is up to date'. Android is unaffected (WorkManager worker path with notifications). The LibraryViewModel only observes the boolean isRefreshing flow, so no layer above can surface the outcome.
evidence: LibraryRefreshRepositoryImpl.kt:125-132 `scope.launch { inlineRefreshing.value = true; try { refreshAllChapters() } finally { inlineRefreshing.value = false } }` — AppResult<Int> ignored; RefreshAllLibraryChaptersUseCase.kt:72 `is AppResult.Failure -> 0 // a single source failing must not abort the whole refresh`.
suggestedFix: Surface the terminal outcome: extend LibraryRefreshRepository with a result flow (e.g. Flow<AppResult<Int>?> of the last run) or change refresh() to suspend returning AppResult<Int> on the inline path, and have LibraryViewModel emit LibraryEffect.ShowError on failure (the effect + :ui mapping already exist).
verifierNote: LibraryRefreshRepositoryImpl.kt:125-132 launches refreshAllChapters() and drops the AppResult<Int>; RefreshAllLibraryChaptersUseCase.kt:72 collapses every per-manga failure to 0, so total failure is indistinguishable from 'up to date' on the Desktop/iOS inline path; only the boolean inlineRefreshing flow is observable. Interface-extending fix is a behavior change → risky correct.

title: Updates Undo restore failure is silent — the row stays permanently deleted while the UI implies the undo succeeded
detail: The delete-with-undo flow deletes the row immediately on OnRequestDelete and re-inserts it on OnUndoDelete via `launchSafely { restoreUpdateEntry(entry) }`. launchSafely's only failure channel is MviViewModel.onUnhandledError, whose default implementation just logs (MviViewModel.kt:178-181) and UpdatesViewModel does not override it in production. If the re-insert throws (Room write failure, disk full), the user who explicitly tapped Undo gets no feedback: pendingDeleteIds was already cleared, the snackbar is gone, the observeUpdates re-emit never brings the row back, and the entry is permanently lost while the interaction read as a successful undo. This is the worst-shaped silent failure among the launchSafely fire-and-forget writes because the action's entire purpose is recovering data the app just destroyed, and there is no other signal (unlike a failed delete, where the row visibly remains).
evidence: UpdatesViewModel.kt:245-250 OnUndoDelete → `launchSafely { restoreUpdateEntry(entry) }` with no failure surfacing; MviViewModel.kt:178-181 default onUnhandledError = Kermit log only.
suggestedFix: In the OnUndoDelete handler, await the restore and emit an error effect on failure (e.g. wrap in runCatchingCancellable and emit UpdatesEffect.ShowError with a typed/localizable error so the user knows the undo failed), or override onUnhandledError in UpdatesViewModel to emit ShowError.
verifierNote: UpdatesViewModel.kt:245-250: OnUndoDelete clears pendingDeleteIds then launchSafely{restoreUpdateEntry}; MviViewModel.kt:158-181 routes the throw to the default onUnhandledError which only Kermit-logs; UpdatesViewModel has no production override (only a test subclass per the comment at line 137). A failed undo is silent and the row is permanently gone — confirmed as described.

title: DilarV2 POST_JSON search body interpolates the raw user query into JSON with no JSON escaping (engine has no JSON-escaped query var)
detail: The DilarV2 search endpoint declares jsonBody {"query":"{query}","includes":["Manga"]}. GenericSourceClient.runRequest expands jsonBody via Templates.expand with vars() where "query" is the RAW search text (GenericSourceClient.kt:524, expansion at :185-188); the only escaping var the engine offers is {queryEncoded} (percent-encoding, semantically wrong inside a JSON string). Consequences: (a) a query containing a double quote (users do quote phrases) produces malformed JSON -> server 4xx -> AppResult.Failure -> a wasted request silently rescued by the legacy fallback; (b) a query containing a backslash followed by a valid JSON escape (\n, \t, \b, \uXXXX, \\) parses as a DIFFERENT term server-side and returns 200 -> wrong-but-Success results that SUPPRESS the legacy fallback — exactly the 'never ship wrong-but-Success' trap the sources-subsystem map documents; (c) the user query can structurally inject extra JSON fields into the request body. This is the only POST_JSON pilot today, so the gap is also a landmine for every future POST_JSON config.
evidence: BundledSourcesConfig.kt:306 "jsonBody": "{\"query\":\"{query}\",\"includes\":[\"Manga\"]}" + GenericSourceClient.kt vars(): '"query" to query' (raw) and '"queryEncoded" to UrlEncode.encode(query)' (percent-encoding only). Templates.expand does plain string substitution with no context-aware escaping.
suggestedFix: Add a JSON-escaped query variable to GenericSourceClient.vars() (e.g. "queryJson" that escapes \" \\ and control chars per RFC 8259), switch the DilarV2 jsonBody to {queryJson}, and have the validator (or a doc note) forbid raw {query} inside jsonBody templates.
verifierNote: BundledSourcesConfig.kt:306 interpolates raw {query} into the jsonBody; GenericSourceClient.vars() (lines 524-525) offers only raw "query" and percent-encoded "queryEncoded" — no JSON-escaping variable exists, and Templates.expand at line 186 is plain substitution. Quote → malformed JSON (4xx), backslash-escape → silently different term with Success that suppresses the legacy fallback. Engine-level queryJson var fix is additive and safe.

title: Library 'Last updated' relative-time renders '0 years ago' for elapsed times of 360-364 days
detail: formatRelativeTime buckets with integer divisions: months = days/30 and years = days/365. For days in 360..364, months == 12 so the 'months < 12' branch fails, and the else branch renders years.toInt() == 0 -> '0 years ago'. The KDoc claims the branches 'mirror the legacy LocalDateTime.timeAgo() helper at composeApp/.../core/util/date/Date.kt:65-99', but that helper gates the months bucket on seconds < 31_536_000 (i.e. < 365 days) and would render '12 months ago' for the same span — the rework diverged at the boundary. A 5-day window every year shows a nonsensical label in the library status line.
evidence: LibraryScreen.kt:1014-1024: months = days / 30; years = days / 365; ... months < 12 -> months_ago; else -> years_ago(years.toInt()). days=360 -> months=12 (branch fails), years=0 -> '0 years ago'. Legacy Date.kt timeAgo: seconds < 31_536_000 -> months bucket (mo up to 12), so no 0-years hole.
suggestedFix: Match the legacy boundary: use 'days < 365 -> stringResource(Res.string.months_ago, months.toInt())' (months then reaches 12, same as legacy) and keep the else branch for days >= 365, or compute years with coerceAtLeast(1) in the else branch.
verifierNote: LibraryScreen.kt:1014-1024: days 360-364 → months=12 fails the months<12 branch, years=days/365=0 → '0 years ago'. Legacy Date.kt timeAgo gates the month bucket on seconds<31_536_000 (=365d) and would render '12 months ago' — so the KDoc's mirror claim (lines 997-999) is wrong at the boundary. Confirmed exactly as written.

title: Template vars that fail to resolve silently expand to "" and yield plausible-but-dead URLs that defeat both isNavigable and the legacy fallback
detail: fieldVars() resolves each template var with '.orEmpty()' (lines 451 and 455-457), so a locator that matches nothing (field drift on the site, or a legitimately-empty array index like DilarV2's chapter.url var releaseId=releases[0].id at BundledSourcesConfig.kt:332) substitutes the empty string into the URL template. The result — e.g. 'https://dilar.tube/api/chapters/' for a chapter whose releases array is empty — is non-blank and does not end in '#', so isNavigable() keeps it and details() returns a Success carrying broken chapter rows. Opening such a chapter 404s, and the FallbackSourceClient pages() fallback cannot recover because the LEGACY client receives the same dead URL. Templates.kt's documented safety ('unknown placeholders are left intact so a malformed template is visible') only covers placeholder-name typos, not empty resolution — a site-side field rename would convert EVERY chapter of a source into uniformly dead URLs while details still looks healthy (the wrong-but-plausible-parse failure mode the campaign's risk profile calls out).
evidence: GenericSourceClient.kt:451 'rootScope?.raw(...).orEmpty()' and :455-457 'parts[0].split(\',\').firstNotNullOfOrNull { ... }.orEmpty()'; isNavigable (line 333) only rejects blank or '#'-suffixed URLs. DilarV2 config: "chapter.url": { "template": "{baseUrl}/api/chapters/{releaseId}", "vars": { "releaseId": "releases[0].id" } }.
suggestedFix: In resolveField(), when a template is used, treat any var that resolves empty (excluding the intentionally-optional root:__dir token) as a field-resolution failure and return "" so the item is dropped by the existing isNavigable filter — or at minimum log via the GenericSourceTest tag so drift is visible. Needs an owner decision on which vars are allowed to be legitimately empty before changing engine behavior.
verifierNote: GenericSourceClient.kt:451/:455-457 resolve template vars with .orEmpty(); a drifted/empty locator yields e.g. 'https://dilar.tube/api/chapters/' which passes isNavigable (line 333 only rejects blank/'#'-suffix), producing Success-carrying dead chapter URLs that the FallbackSourceClient cannot rescue (legacy receives the same URL). Matches the campaign's wrong-but-plausible-parse risk; engine behavior change needs the owner call on legitimately-empty vars → risky correct.

title: Desktop Coil image client is a bare HttpClient{} on CIO — inherits CIO's default 15s whole-request timeout that Android's twin deliberately forbids
detail: The Desktop (and iOS) actuals build the Coil network client as `HttpClient { }` with only the page-progress observer installed — no HttpTimeout configuration at all. On Desktop the engine resolved at runtime is CIO (the only JVM engine on the classpath, confirmed by the file's own KDoc line 22), and CIOEngineConfig ships a DEFAULT WHOLE-REQUEST TIMEOUT of 15 000 ms. The Android twin (PlatformNetworkFetcher.android.kt:83-89) configures 30s connect / 60s read / 60s write, retryOnConnectionFailure(true), pingInterval(15s) and — per the explicit comment in all three HttpClientFactory actuals — 'requestTimeoutMillis is intentionally omitted: a slow-but-progressing large response must not be aborted'. Result: every Coil image fetch on Desktop (covers AND reader pages — this factory feeds the singleton ImageLoader in App.kt:358-366) is hard-aborted after 15 seconds total, so tall manga pages on slow networks consistently fail on Desktop where Android succeeds. The Desktop client also has no retry and none of the 200MB disk-cache parity the Android twin documents as load-bearing. Bonus staleness: App.kt:364's comment 'on Desktop/iOS we leave it null so Coil's ServiceLoader picks ktor3' is false — both actuals now return a non-null factory built on this bare client. The iOS twin (PlatformNetworkFetcher.ios.kt:58) has the same bare-client shape (Darwin defaults apply: 60s inactivity, no connect timeout control, no retry) — less acute but equally unconfigured.
evidence: Desktop actual: `val client = HttpClient { }.apply { installPageProgressObserver(...) }` — no `install(HttpTimeout)`. CIO default: `CIOEngineConfig.requestTimeout = 15_000` (whole-request). Android actual: `.connectTimeout(30,SECONDS).readTimeout(60,SECONDS).writeTimeout(60,SECONDS).retryOnConnectionFailure(true)` plus the repo-wide design note 'requestTimeoutMillis is intentionally omitted ... a slow-but-progressing large response must not be aborted' (HttpClientFactory.android.kt:38-43).
suggestedFix: In both the Desktop and iOS actuals, configure the client to match the documented native contract: `HttpClient { install(HttpTimeout) { connectTimeoutMillis = 30_000; socketTimeoutMillis = 60_000 } }` (leaving requestTimeoutMillis unset disables CIO's 15s default because the plugin overrides engine timeouts), and update the stale App.kt:364 comment. Optionally add HttpCache for cover re-download parity.
verifierNote: Desktop actual is `HttpClient { }` with no HttpTimeout (PlatformNetworkFetcher.desktop.kt:32); the only JVM ktor engine is CIO (shared/build.gradle.kts:205, desktopMain) whose CIOEngineConfig.requestTimeout defaults to 15_000ms whole-request (known to abort long streaming bodies); Android twin sets 30/60/60+retry (android.kt:85-89) and all HttpClientFactory actuals document 'requestTimeoutMillis intentionally omitted'. App.kt:364 'we leave it null so ServiceLoader picks ktor3' comment is indeed stale (factory is non-null). Slow tall-page fetches on Desktop hard-fail at 15s → major.

title: Reader page-share crashes on iPad: UIActivityViewController presented without a popover anchor (app targets device family 1,2)
detail: shareBitmapBytes presents a UIActivityViewController via `rootVC?.presentViewController(activityVC, ...)` without ever touching `activityVC.popoverPresentationController`. On iPad, UIActivityViewController is presented as a popover and UIKit throws an NSGenericException ('UIPopoverPresentationController should have a non-nil sourceView or barButtonItem set before the presentation occurs') the moment presentation occurs. The surrounding `catch (e: Exception)` does NOT help: this is an Objective-C NSException raised inside UIKit, which Kotlin/Native cannot catch with a Kotlin try/catch — it terminates the process. The iOS app explicitly targets iPad: iosApp/project.yml sets `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY: "1,2"`. The method is live: it is the reader's share-current-page action (ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute.kt:152-154 and its legacy-args twin call `screenshotProvider.shareBitmapBytes(bytes, ...)`). So tapping share in the reader on any iPad hard-crashes the app. Distinct from the already-known finding on this file (keyWindow-nil/main-thread silent no-op) — this is a guaranteed ObjC-exception crash on a supported device family.
evidence: `val activityVC = UIActivityViewController(activityItems = listOf(image), applicationActivities = null)` ... `rootVC?.presentViewController(activityVC, animated = true, completion = null)` — no popoverPresentationController configuration; project.yml: `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY: "1,2"`.
suggestedFix: Before presenting, anchor the popover for pad idiom: `activityVC.popoverPresentationController?.let { pop -> pop.sourceView = rootVC.view; pop.sourceRect = CGRectMake(rootVC.view.bounds.useContents{size.width}/2.0, rootVC.view.bounds.useContents{size.height}/2.0, 0.0, 0.0); pop.permittedArrowDirections = 0u }` (popoverPresentationController is non-nil only when a popover presentation would be used, so this is a no-op on iPhone).
verifierNote: Verified live, not latent: PlatformModule.ios.kt:137 binds single<ScreenshotProvider>{ IosScreenshotProvider() } and ChapterImagesReworkScreenRoute.kt:97/157 injects exactly that :platform interface for the reader share action. shareBitmapBytes (IosScreenshotProvider.kt:48-60) never touches popoverPresentationController, project.yml:31 targets device family "1,2", and the UIKit NSGenericException on iPad cannot be caught by the Kotlin try/catch (ObjC exception terminates the process). Deterministic crash on a normal user action on a supported device family → upgraded major→critical per the crash rubric.

title: iOS/Desktop connectivity is 'can I reach Google', and Details hard-gates downloads on it — false permanent offline on Google-blocked networks
detail: Android's ConnectivityObserver reports OS network state (ConnectivityManager callbacks). The Desktop and iOS impls instead HEAD-probe `https://www.google.com/generate_204` every 5 seconds and report Unavailable on any failure. ConnectivityRepositoryImpl collapses this to `isOnline`, and DetailsViewModel hard-gates BOTH the single-chapter and download-all paths on it (DetailsViewModel.kt:674, 796: `if (!state.value.isOnline) { emit(ShowError(AppError.Network.NoConnectivity())); return }`). Consequence: on any network where google.com is unreachable — Google-blocked regions (e.g. China, Iran — a plausible audience for an Arabic-heavy manga app), corporate filters, DNS-blocking captive portals — iOS/Desktop users can browse and read sources normally but every download attempt is rejected with 'No connectivity', permanently, with no override. Android is unaffected. Side effect: the probe also leaks 'app is running' beacons to Google every 5s for the lifetime of any Details screen. The two existing known findings on these files (redundant `|| code == 204`; per-collector loop/client leak on iOS) do not cover this false-negative gating semantics.
evidence: DesktopConnectivityObserver: `DEFAULT_PROBE_URL = "https://www.google.com/generate_204"`, `catch (_: Throwable) { Status.Unavailable }`; IosConnectivityObserver.kt:58-66 identical posture; ConnectivityRepositoryImpl maps `it == Status.Available`; DetailsViewModel gates downloads on `state.value.isOnline`.
suggestedFix: Use OS-level reachability instead of a Google probe: NWPathMonitor on iOS, `NetworkInterface.getNetworkInterfaces()` up-check or a probe against the ACTIVE SOURCE's host on Desktop. At minimum treat probe failure as 'unknown' rather than offline for the download gate (fail-open), or make the probe URL the active source's baseUrl.
verifierNote: DesktopConnectivityObserver.kt:46-66 HEAD-probes google.com/generate_204 every 5s and maps any throw to Unavailable; IosConnectivityObserver has the same posture (line 66); ConnectivityRepositoryImpl.kt:21 collapses to `== Available`; DetailsViewModel.kt:674/:796 hard-gate both download paths with no override. On Google-unreachable networks (plausible for this app's audience) downloads are permanently rejected as offline on iOS/Desktop while browsing works. Not an accepted-stub gap — it's wrong gating semantics. Major/risky stand.

title: iOS notification authorization is never requested anywhere — two files' KDocs claim 'the iOS app shell triggers it at launch', but iOSApp.swift only bootstraps Koin
detail: Both this actual's KDoc ('the iOS app shell triggers [requestAuthorizationWithOptions] at launch — outside this Composable's scope') and IosNotificationPresenter.kt's KDoc ('Permission prompting belongs to the bootstrap path') delegate UNUserNotificationCenter authorization to the app shell — but no call to requestAuthorizationWithOptions exists anywhere in the repo (verified: grep over all .swift and .kt sources matches only KDoc prose; iOSApp.swift's init only calls IosKoinKt.bootstrapIosKoin()). Consequences: (1) this actual models permission as granted (`MutableStateFlow(true)`) on a false premise, so the Theme-onboarding notification step on iOS reports 'granted' without any prompt ever being shown; (2) IosNotificationPresenter.show() posts UNNotificationRequests that will be rejected as unauthorized, and the addNotificationRequest completion handler swallows the error — so if any flow ever posts a notification on iOS it is silently dropped. Today NotificationPresenter has no live caller on iOS (bound in PlatformModule.ios.kt:110 but never injected), so the impact is latent — but both KDocs assert infrastructure that does not exist, and the audit postscript (Task #618) even claims it was 'verified'.
evidence: `grep -rn requestAuthorization composeApp iosApp platform shared` → only KDoc/comment lines; iOSApp.swift init: `IosKoinKt.bootstrapIosKoin()` and nothing else; IosNotificationPresenter.show(): `addNotificationRequest(request) { _ -> /* errors swallowed */ }`.
suggestedFix: Either add the authorization request to the iOS bootstrap (e.g. in iOSApp.init or MainViewController, call UNUserNotificationCenter.requestAuthorizationWithOptions(alert|sound|badge)) and drive `hasPermission` from getNotificationSettings, or correct both KDocs to state that authorization is not requested and notifications are inert on iOS.
verifierNote: Repo-wide grep for requestAuthorization matches only KDoc prose (RememberNotificationPermissionRequester.ios.kt:13, IosNotificationPresenter.kt:14, NotificationPermissionRequester.kt:9); iOSApp.swift's init only calls IosKoinKt.bootstrapIosKoin(). The iOS actual hard-codes hasPermission=MutableStateFlow(true) on the false 'app shell triggers it at launch' premise; NotificationPresenter is bound (PlatformModule.ios.kt:110) but has no common-code caller, so impact is latent. Confirmed as written.

title: iOS/Desktop HttpCache comment claims the manhastro /dados 1-day cache window is honored — but the Cache-Control header is stamped by an Android-only OkHttp interceptor
detail: Both HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:40-42 and HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt:41-43 install HttpCache with the comment 'so Cache-Control directives (incl. the 1-day window for manhastro /dados) are honored, mirroring source's OkHttp cache on Android'. But that 1-day window does not come from the server — it is stamped onto responses by the `forceCacheForDados()` OkHttp NETWORK interceptor that exists only in HttpClientFactory.android.kt:15-27 (the native app added that interceptor precisely because the server does not emit cacheable headers; the dead commonMain helper forceCacheForDados.kt documents the same intent). With no equivalent response-header rewrite on iOS/Desktop, HttpCache has nothing to cache for /dados, so the heavy Manhastro /dados payload is re-fetched on every call on those platforms — a silent native-parity gap hidden behind a comment asserting the opposite.
evidence: iOS/Desktop: `install(HttpCache)` + comment citing 'the 1-day window for manhastro /dados'; Android-only: `addNetworkInterceptor(forceCacheForDados())` rewriting `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` onto `https://api2.manhastro.net/dados*` responses.
suggestedFix: Port the /dados Cache-Control stamping to the shared client via a Ktor HttpResponsePipeline/Sender interceptor on iOS/Desktop (rewrite the response headers for the DADOS_URL_PREFIX before HttpCache sees them), or — minimally — fix the two comments to say /dados caching is Android-only.
verifierNote: iOS/Desktop install(HttpCache) comments (HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:40-42) credit the manhastro /dados 1-day window, but the Cache-Control stamping lives only in the Android-only OkHttp network interceptor (HttpClientFactory.android.kt:25-35); the commonMain Ktor port attachForceCacheForDados() exists but grep shows it is never called anywhere — so /dados responses are uncacheable on iOS/Desktop and the comment asserts the opposite. Confirmed.

title: iOS user-id falls back to empty string when identifierForVendor is nil — complaint ownership merges across all affected users
detail: The three UserIdProvider actuals disagree on the nil/failure fallback: Android returns the sentinel 'Unable to retrieve Android ID', Desktop generates and PERSISTS a UUID (device-id file), iOS returns `""`. identifierForVendor is documented to be nil in rare windows (e.g. after device restart before first unlock). A complaint submitted then carries userId="" (FeedbackRepositoryImpl.kt:138), and ComplaintListRepositoryImpl.kt:132 lists 'my complaints' by that same id — so every user who ever hit the nil window shares one identity: they see, reply to, and (via the unauthenticated REST update path already on file) can edit each other's complaints. Also unlike Desktop, the iOS id is not persisted, so vendor-id rotation (uninstall of all vendor apps) silently orphans a user's complaint history while Desktop survives.
evidence: iOS: `identifierForVendor?.UUIDString ?: ""`; Desktop: persisted `UUID.randomUUID()` in ~/.yami-manga/device-id; Android: `?: "Unable to retrieve Android ID"`.
suggestedFix: Mirror the Desktop posture on iOS: on first call, if identifierForVendor is nil (or as a general strategy), generate a UUID and persist it in NSUserDefaults/Keychain; never return empty string.
verifierNote: Verified the three-way fallback divergence: iOS `identifierForVendor?.UUIDString ?: ""` (IosUserIdProvider.kt:16), Desktop persisted UUID in ~/.yami-manga/device-id, Android sentinel string; FeedbackRepositoryImpl.kt:138 stamps complaints with that userId and ComplaintListRepositoryImpl.kt:132 lists 'my complaints' by it, so all nil-IDFV users share the "" identity. Rare trigger window keeps it minor; NSUserDefaults/Keychain-persisted UUID fix is iOS-additive and safe.

title: Test pins the confirmed-broken observeBookmark single-emit-then-complete behavior via awaitComplete()
detail: observeBookmark_emits_false_when_chapter_not_in_library asserts `awaitComplete()` after the single `false` emission. This pins exactly the behavior already confirmed as a bug in known finding 'ChapterBookmarkRepositoryImpl.kt:42 — observeBookmark completes after a single false when the chapter row doesn't exist; bookmark state never re-binds if the row appears later' (e.g. the user adds the manga to the library while the reader is open). The test elevates the broken completion semantics to a documented contract: fixing the impl (keeping the flow alive / re-binding on row appearance) will fail this test, and a future maintainer reading the test will conclude the early completion is intentional.
suggestedFix: Assert only the false emission and stop pinning termination: replace `awaitComplete()` with `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()` plus a comment referencing the open re-bind gap; update the test to assert re-binding once ChapterBookmarkRepositoryImpl.observeBookmark is fixed.
verifierNote: Confirmed the pin: ReaderStranglerDataTest.kt:95-98 asserts awaitComplete() after the single false, which is exactly ChapterBookmarkRepositoryImpl.kt:42-49's emit(false)-then-complete no-rebind behavior flagged in the known finding. fixSafety corrected risky→safe: the suggested change (cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents + comment) is a test-only edit that still passes against the current impl and stops pinning the broken contract.

title: cancellationException_isNotSwallowed test cannot detect swallowing — it stays green if the rethrow is removed
detail: The test's name and inline comment claim to verify that a CancellationException out of handle() 'must propagate (cooperative cancellation / VM-clear must work) — NOT be routed to onUnhandledError'. But its assertions (`assertNull(vm.caught)` + VM still processes the next intent) only cover the second half. If MviViewModel.submit's `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` were regressed to swallow the exception silently (catch and ignore), both assertions would still pass — the hook is not invoked and the VM keeps working either way. The propagation guarantee the test is named after is structurally unverified, giving false regression coverage for the cancel-before-relaunch Job pattern the codebase relies on (ReaderViewModel etc.).
suggestedFix: Strengthen the test to observe propagation, e.g. exercise the pattern through launchSafely (which returns the Job) and assert `job.isCancelled` after a CancellationException, or have handle() set a flag in a `finally` and assert the coroutine completed exceptionally; at minimum rename the test to reflect what is actually asserted (does-not-route-to-hook).
verifierNote: Verified against MviViewModelSafetyNetTest.kt:72-81: the only assertions are assertNull(vm.caught) and the follow-up intent processing — both hold equally if submit()'s `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` were regressed to a silent swallow (hook not invoked either way, and a fresh coroutine per submit keeps the VM usable). The named propagation guarantee is structurally unasserted; strengthening/renaming is test-only and safe.

title: Real-filesystem temp dirs are only cleaned up when the test passes; RecordingFs records nothing
detail: All three tests build a RecordingFs over the REAL FileSystem.SYSTEM under SYSTEM_TEMPORARY_DIRECTORY (`yami-remove-test-<rand>`), seed manga directories, and call `appFs.cleanUp()` as the LAST statement of the test body — after the assertions. Any assertion failure (or an exception out of the repo under test) skips cleanUp, leaking seeded directories on the developer/CI machine on every red run; the random suffix means they accumulate rather than overwrite. Additionally the helper is named `RecordingFs` but records nothing (no call log) — a stale copy-paste name that misleads readers about what the fake does.
evidence:
val appFs = RecordingFs().apply { seedManga(7L) }
...
assertEquals(listOf("c/1"), readProgress.cleared, ...)
appFs.cleanUp()  // skipped entirely when any assert above throws
suggestedFix: Hold the RecordingFs in a field created per-test and delete it in an @AfterTest method (or wrap each test body in try/finally { appFs.cleanUp() }); rename RecordingFs to TempDirFs or similar since it records nothing.
verifierNote: All three tests in LibraryRepositoryRemoveTest.kt (lines 138, 173, 208) call appFs.cleanUp() as the last statement after the asserts, over the REAL FileSystem.SYSTEM under a random-suffixed SYSTEM_TEMPORARY_DIRECTORY root — any red run leaks the seeded dirs, and they accumulate. RecordingFs (lines 93-101) indeed records nothing (no call log). @AfterTest/try-finally + rename is test-only and safe.

title: Firestore ComplaintDto is serialized reflectively with no R8 keep rule — minified release builds write obfuscated (or zero) field names to the complaints_v2 collection
detail: ComplaintFirestoreDataSource.sendComplaint/updateComplaint pass a Kotlin data class (private ComplaintDto, ComplaintFirestoreDataSource.kt:330) straight to Firestore's .add(dto)/.set(dto). The Android Firestore SDK maps POJOs via reflection (CustomClassMapper reads getter names at runtime). :app builds release with isMinifyEnabled=true and android.enableR8.fullMode=true, and neither app/proguard-rules.pro nor Firestore's consumer rules (verified: firebase-firestore-26.0.2.aar proguard.txt contains only -dontwarn lines, no POJO keeps) keep this class's members. Since the DTO's getters are never called from code (only its constructor is), R8 full mode will either strip the getters entirely (CustomClassMapper then throws 'No properties to serialize found' — sendComplaint crashes release-only) or rename them (complaints get written with meaningless single-letter field names that don't match what the read path and the admin panel query). The codebase itself proves this exact failure already shipped in the native app: the read path compensates for legacy obfuscated field names 'a'..'g' (lines 67-95: Filter.equalTo("a", ...), doc.getString("b")...). A new R8 run produces a *different* mapping, so newly-written release complaints would not even match those legacy fallbacks. Debug builds (no minify) never show this.
evidence: ComplaintFirestoreDataSource.kt:52 `complaintsCol.add(dto)`, :162 `.set(dto)`, :330 `private data class ComplaintDto(val userId: String...)`; read-side legacy-obfuscation fallbacks at :67-95 (`Filter.equalTo("a", trimmedUserId)`, `doc.getString("type") ?: doc.getString("b")`); app/build.gradle.kts:96 `isMinifyEnabled = true`; gradle.properties:14 `android.enableR8.fullMode=true`; app/proguard-rules.pro has no rule covering me.manga.yamiapk.presentation.** or the DTO.
suggestedFix: Add to app/proguard-rules.pro: `-keepclassmembers class me.manga.yamiapk.presentation.features.complaint.repository.ComplaintFirestoreDataSource$ComplaintDto { <init>(...); <fields>; <methods>; }` (or `-keep` the class outright). Longer-term: annotate each property with @PropertyName (which Firestore consumer rules then protect) or write an explicit Map<String,Any> instead of a reflective POJO.
verifierNote: Verified: ComplaintFirestoreDataSource.kt:52/:162 pass the private ComplaintDto (:330, reflective POJO, getters never called in code) to add()/set(); app/proguard-rules.pro has no rule covering it (only work/, crash/, dao/, entity/, ViewModel, generated-resources keeps); extracted firebase-firestore-26.0.2.aar proguard.txt and it is indeed only -dontwarn lines; app/build.gradle.kts:96 isMinifyEnabled=true + gradle.properties:14 R8 fullMode. The DataSource is live (PlatformModule.android.kt:226 binding). Release-only serialize failure/renamed fields is real; suggested keepclassmembers rule targets the correct FQCN.

title: Kermit release log floor (Warn) is applied only on Android — shipped iOS and Desktop builds emit Info/Debug logs including Cookie/cf_clearance header values and full scraper diagnostics
detail: MyApp.kt:155-161 raises the global Kermit floor to Severity.Warn in non-debug builds, with an explicit SECURITY comment that legacy scraper Info logs 'can include request URLs, header maps (Cookie/cf_clearance/User-Agent values), and full HTML bodies'. That floor is set in the Android host only. The iOS bootstrap (KoinHelper.doInitKoin, called from iOSApp.swift) and the Desktop bootstrap (desktopApp Main.kt:79 initKoin(...)) never call Logger.setMinSeverity (repo-wide grep: the only call site is MyApp.kt:160). Kermit's default min severity is Verbose, so an App Store iOS build logs every scraper Info line to os_log — readable in Console.app on any tethered Mac — and a packaged Desktop build prints them to stdout. Concrete leaking lines exist and are platform-shared (commonMain): BatcaveRepository.kt:133 logs the resolved Cookie header value at Info, WebtoontrRepository.kt:42 logs the full per-source header map ('Headers from DataStore: $headers') at Info, NormalSites.kt:100 logHeaders(). The cf_clearance cookie is a session credential for bypassing Cloudflare. Same gap also keeps the high-volume FlowLog Debug trace live in shipped iOS/Desktop builds (string building cost on every reader/library event).
evidence: grep for setMinSeverity across all modules returns only app/src/main/java/me/manga/yamiapk/MyApp.kt:160 (gated on BuildConfig.DEBUG). KoinHelper.kt:19 fun doInitKoin and desktopApp Main.kt:79 initKoin(allReworkModules()) configure no logger floor. Leak sources in commonMain (run on all platforms): shared/.../en/batcave/BatcaveRepository.kt:133 `Logger.withTag(TAG).i { "initSite: Cookie header resolved: $cookieHeaderValue" }`, shared/.../tr/webtoontr/WebtoontrRepository.kt:42 `.i { "Headers from DataStore: $headers" }`.
suggestedFix: Mirror the Android floor in the other two hosts: in doInitKoin (or iOSApp.swift before doInitKoin) set Logger.setMinSeverity(Severity.Warn) when !Platform.isDebugBinary (the same signal HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:22 already uses); in desktopApp Main.kt apply the floor when the app is not started with assertions/-ea (reuse the desiredAssertionStatus() probe from HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt) or when packaged.
verifierNote: Repo-wide grep confirms the only Logger.setMinSeverity call is MyApp.kt:160 (Android, !BuildConfig.DEBUG); KoinHelper.doInitKoin (iosMain:19) and desktopApp Main.kt:79 set no floor, so Kermit's Verbose default applies on shipped iOS/Desktop. Leak sources verified in commonMain: BatcaveRepository.kt:133 logs the resolved Cookie header value at Info, WebtoontrRepository.kt:42 logs the full DataStore header map, NormalSites.kt:100 logHeaders(). Suggested signals (Platform.isDebugBinary at HttpClientFactory.ios.kt:22, desiredAssertionStatus at HttpClientFactory.desktop.kt:23) both exist.

title: CrashActivity keep rule's member spec matches nothing: start() is a companion-object function, not a static method
detail: The rule keeps `public static void start(android.content.Context, java.lang.String)` on me.manga.yamiapk.crash.CrashActivity, with a comment saying the static helper must 'survive R8's static-inlining pass'. But CrashActivity.start (CrashActivity.kt:38) is declared in a companion object without @JvmStatic, so it compiles to CrashActivity$Companion.start(...) — there is no static `start` on CrashActivity for the rule to match, and ProGuard member specs that match nothing are silently ignored. Nothing breaks today only because the sole call site (MyApp's uncaught-exception handler) keeps the method reachable statically; the rule's documented protection is a no-op and would not help if the call site ever became reflective.
evidence: app/proguard-rules.pro:90-93 keeps `public static void start(...)`; CrashActivity.kt:35-38 `companion object { ... fun start(context: Context, stacktrace: String)` with no @JvmStatic.
suggestedFix: Either add @JvmStatic to CrashActivity.Companion.start so the rule matches, or change the rule to `-keepclassmembers class me.manga.yamiapk.crash.CrashActivity$Companion { public void start(android.content.Context, java.lang.String); }` (and keep the Companion field on the outer class).
verifierNote: CrashActivity.kt:36-46 declares start(Context, String) in a companion object with no @JvmStatic, so it compiles to CrashActivity$Companion.start — the proguard-rules.pro:90-93 member spec 'public static void start(...)' matches nothing and is silently ignored. Harmless today (MyApp.kt:116 call site keeps it reachable; the class+<init> keep still applies), so minor dead-rule finding is correct.

title: versionCode 35 / versionName 1.0.35 are identical to the native app being replaced — the KMP build cannot ship as an update to the same applicationId
detail: The KMP :app uses applicationId me.manga.yamiapk with versionCode 35 / versionName 1.0.35 — exactly the values in native-app/app/build.gradle.kts (:29-33). Since the port targets the same listing/install base (same applicationId, 100% parity goal), any release artifact built from this config is rejected by Play ('version code already used') and by `adb install -r` over an existing native install. Version-gated in-app features (the What's-New show-once gate keys on the version string) would also treat the port as 'already seen'. Needs a deliberate bump (e.g. 36/1.0.36) as part of the release checklist; the choice of scheme is the owner's.
evidence: app/build.gradle.kts:62-63 `versionCode = 35 / versionName = "1.0.35"`; native-app/app/build.gradle.kts:29-33 `applicationId "me.manga.yamiapk" / versionCode = 35 / versionName = "1.0.35"`.
suggestedFix: Bump versionCode/versionName above the native app's shipped values before any release build; consider deriving them from a single gradle.properties entry shared with desktopAppVersion (desktopApp/build.gradle.kts:55) and iosApp Info.plist (CFBundleVersion 35), which currently triplicate the same hardcoded 1.0.35.
verifierNote: app/build.gradle.kts:59-63 (applicationId me.manga.yamiapk, versionCode 35, versionName 1.0.35) is byte-identical to native-app/app/build.gradle.kts:29-33 — Play and adb install -r both reject same-versionCode updates to the same applicationId. Release-checklist item, correctly report-only (version scheme is the owner's call).

title: Desktop macOS packaging never sets macOS.bundleID — CFBundleIdentifier defaults to the display name 'Yami Manga' (space, not reverse-DNS), inconsistent with me.manga.yamiapk elsewhere
detail: nativeDistributions configures only targetFormats/packageName/packageVersion. The Compose plugin's macOS notarization/app-dir path defaults bundleID to packageName (AbstractNativeMacApplicationPackageAppDirTask.kt:33 in compose-gradle-plugin 1.11.0: `bundleID ... .value(packageName)`), i.e. 'Yami Manga' — which violates Apple's CFBundleIdentifier charset (alphanumerics, hyphens, periods only) — and the plain packageDmg path lets jpackage derive its own identifier from the main class. Either way the macOS app identity is unpinned and disagrees with the Android applicationId / iOS PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER (both me.manga.yamiapk). This bites the moment the dmg is signed/notarized for distribution (signing validation requires a valid, stable bundle id) and makes per-app macOS state (TCC grants, preferences identity) unstable across packaging-path changes.
evidence: desktopApp/build.gradle.kts:95-99 has no macOS { } block; plugin source AbstractNativeMacApplicationPackageAppDirTask.kt:33 `val bundleID: Property<String> = objects.notNullProperty<String>().value(packageName)`; iosApp/project.yml:27 and app/build.gradle.kts:59 pin me.manga.yamiapk.
suggestedFix: Add inside nativeDistributions: `macOS { bundleID = "me.manga.yamiapk" }` (optionally also dockName/iconFile while there).
verifierNote: Gap is real — desktopApp/build.gradle.kts:95-99 has no macOS{bundleID} block, so the macOS app identity is unpinned and inconsistent with me.manga.yamiapk (Android/iOS), and signing/notarization needs a stable reverse-DNS id — but the cited mechanism is wrong: AbstractNativeMacApplicationPackageAppDirTask (bundleID := packageName) is the experimental Kotlin/Native packaging path, not JVM nativeDistributions. Decompiled compose-gradle-plugin 1.10.0: the jpackage task only passes --mac-package-identifier when macOS.bundleID is set (ConfigureJvmApplicationKt lambda$93$lambda$89 reads getBundleID(), cliArg skips null), so jpackage derives the identifier from the main class name, not 'Yami Manga'. Suggested fix (set bundleID) is correct.

title: The documented release path-validation flow (-PallowPlaceholderGoogleServices=true) still hard-fails without a production keystore — release signing has no fallback
detail: The release guard at lines 25-52 explicitly supports building release artifacts 'for build-PATH validation only (CI release-verify, local R8 smoke)' via -PallowPlaceholderGoogleServices=true. But buildTypes.release unconditionally sets signingConfig = signingConfigs['release'], whose storeFile falls back to a non-existent local file ('yami-release.keystore' is not in the repo — verified via git ls-files) and whose passwords come only from env/properties. Without KEYSTORE_* env vars the build dies at validateSigningRelease before R8 ever runs, so the very flow the guard documents (local R8 smoke to catch the release-only crashes this lens is about, e.g. r4-build-1) is not actually executable. Given minify/shrink are release-only, no contributor can exercise R8 locally without obtaining the production keystore.
evidence: app/build.gradle.kts:68-77 signingConfigs.release with `storeFile = file(envKeystoreFile ?: localKeystore)`; :86 `signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")` unconditional; no yami-release.keystore tracked in git; guard comment at :23-24 promises an R8-smoke path.
suggestedFix: Fall back to the debug signing config when the release keystore is absent, e.g. `signingConfig = if (signingConfigs.getByName("release").storeFile?.exists() == true) signingConfigs.getByName("release") else signingConfigs.getByName("debug")` (optionally only when allowPlaceholderGoogleServices is set, and print a loud warning).
verifierNote: Verified: buildTypes.release unconditionally sets signingConfigs.release (app/build.gradle.kts:86), whose storeFile falls back to yami-release.keystore which is neither tracked (git ls-files) nor present on disk — so the guard's documented -PallowPlaceholderGoogleServices=true R8-smoke path (:23-24) still dies at validateSigningRelease without KEYSTORE_* env. Mitigation exists (running :app:minifyReleaseWithR8 directly skips signing), so minor; the debug-signing fallback fix is correctly marked risky (accidental debug-signed release artifacts).

title: Flexible in-app update is started but can never complete: completeUpdate() has zero callers and DOWNLOADED is never handled
detail: startInAppUpdateFlow() only does checkForUpdate() -> startFlexibleUpdate(). Nothing in the entire repo calls AppUpdateClient.completeUpdate() (grep: only the interface and the iOS/Desktop no-op actuals mention it), there is no InstallStateUpdatedListener, and MainActivity has no onResume re-check. So when the user accepts the Play flexible-update dialog, the new APK downloads (data cost) and is never installed. Worse, AndroidAppUpdateClient.checkForUpdate() returns null for any availability other than UPDATE_AVAILABLE (AndroidAppUpdateClient.kt:39), so once the download is in progress/finished (DEVELOPER_TRIGGERED_UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS), subsequent launches do nothing either — the downloaded update is stranded forever. Native parity is explicit: native MainActivity registers AppUpdateHelper.registerListener(onDownloaded = { AppUpdateHelper.completeUpdate() }) at onCreate and calls AppUpdateHelper.resumeUpdate -> completeUpdate() in onResume (native-app MainActivity.kt:304-312, 883-895). PLATFORM_FEATURE_MATRIX.md grades Android in-app update as 'full', which this contradicts.
evidence: MainActivity.kt:86-89 `if (client.checkForUpdate() != null) { client.startFlexibleUpdate() }` — the only update call sites in the app; `grep -rn completeUpdate` across app/composeApp/presentation/shared returns no production caller; AndroidAppUpdateClient.kt:39 `if (info.updateAvailability() != UpdateAvailability.UPDATE_AVAILABLE) return null`.
suggestedFix: Extend AppUpdateClient with an install-state callback (or a suspend awaitDownloaded()) wired to Play Core's InstallStateUpdatedListener; in MainActivity call completeUpdate() when state hits DOWNLOADED, and on each onResume check appUpdateInfo.installStatus() == DOWNLOADED and complete (mirroring native's registerListener + resumeUpdate).
verifierNote: Verified: MainActivity.kt:86-89 only checkForUpdate→startFlexibleUpdate; repo grep finds no production completeUpdate caller (only the SPI at AppUpdateClient.kt:30 and the iOS/Desktop no-ops); no InstallStateUpdatedListener or onResume re-check anywhere; AndroidAppUpdateClient.kt returns null for any availability != UPDATE_AVAILABLE, stranding an in-progress/downloaded update. Native parity confirmed: native MainActivity.kt:304-311 registerListener(onDownloaded={completeUpdate()}) + :883-895 onResume resumeUpdate→completeUpdate. PLATFORM_FEATURE_MATRIX.md:45 grades Android in-app update 'full', contradicted. The SPI KDoc even claims the result plumbing 'stays in the Android host's Activity callback wiring' — the host has none.

title: Unconditional MobileAds.initialize() at process start makes MainActivity's UMP canRequestAds() gate dead code
detail: MyApp.onCreate step 5 calls MobileAds.initialize(this) on every process start, before any UMP consent interaction is possible. MainActivity.startConsentFlow() then carefully gates a second MobileAds.initialize on consent.canRequestAds() with the comment 'Native calls MobileAds.initialize only once consent permits ad requests' — but SDK initialization is once-per-process, so that gate guards a no-op: the Google Mobile Ads SDK (plus the bundled IronSource mediation adapter, app/build.gradle.kts:168) is already initialized for every user, including EEA users who have not consented or who declined. Google's UMP integration contract is to initialize the Mobile Ads SDK only after canRequestAds() is true. The quirk does match native (native MyApp.kt also initializes unconditionally), but it is harmful (GDPR/Play data-collection posture) and it silently falsifies the consent-gating the KMP MainActivity claims to implement — worth an owner decision rather than silent inheritance.
evidence: MyApp.kt:168-172 `MobileAds.initialize(this) { ... }` (unconditional, runs before MainActivity exists); MainActivity.kt:103-108 `if (consent.canRequestAds()) { ... MobileAds.initialize(...) }` — second init is a per-process no-op.
suggestedFix: Delete the MobileAds.initialize call from MyApp.onCreate and let the consent-gated init in MainActivity.startConsentFlow() be the only initialization path (single-line removal; ads are currently dormant so there is no behavioral downside). Document the deliberate divergence from native.
verifierNote: Facts confirmed: MyApp.kt:168-172 initializes MobileAds unconditionally at process start, making MainActivity.kt:103-108's canRequestAds()-gated second init a per-process no-op. But native MyApp.kt:52 does exactly the same, so per the APP_MAP parity rule this is inherited native behavior, ads are dormant, and the harm is compliance posture (not user-visible incorrectness) — severity downgraded to minor as an owner-decision note. The misleading gate/comment in MainActivity is the concrete code smell.

title: Consent and review flows launched on Dispatchers.IO from onCreate race ActivityHolder, which is only populated in onActivityResumed — UMP form can silently never show
detail: startConsentFlow() and startInAppReviewFlow() launch on Dispatchers.IO directly from onCreate. Both facades resolve their Activity via `{ ActivityHolder.current }` (PlatformModule.android.kt:158-160), and ActivityHolder is set only in MyApp's onActivityResumed callback (MyApp.kt:184). The IO coroutine typically starts executing while the main thread is still finishing the create/start/resume lifecycle transaction, so AndroidConsentFlowClient.requestConsentInfoUpdate() hits its `activityProvider() ?: return ConsentStatus.UNKNOWN` branch (AndroidConsentFlowClient.kt:43) and loadAndShowConsentFormIfRequired() returns false — all logged at warn and never retried for the session, because the flows run once per onCreate. Net effect: on cold starts that lose the race, a first-run EEA user is never shown the UMP consent form, canRequestAds() stays false, and (once ads are actually wired) ad serving is permanently disabled for them, all silently. The class KDoc's claim that 'by the time these run (post-setContent, on resume) this Activity is the current foreground one' is only true for the Main-dispatched update flow, whose runnable is queued behind the lifecycle transaction; IO dispatch has no such ordering. Native had no race: it passed `this@MainActivity` into requestConsent/launchInAppReview directly. (Secondary note: UMP's form APIs are main-thread APIs; invoking them from an IO thread relies on the SDK's internal main-thread posting.)
evidence: MainActivity.kt:98 `launchFlowScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { ... consent.requestConsentInfoUpdate()` and :129 same pattern for review; ActivityHolder.set only called from `onActivityResumed` (MyApp.kt:184); AndroidConsentFlowClient.kt:43-46 returns UNKNOWN when the provider yields null.
suggestedFix: Don't rely on ActivityHolder for the launch flows of the Activity that is itself starting them: either delay the IO flows until after first resume (e.g. lifecycleScope.launch { lifecycle.withResumed { } } / repeatOnLifecycle(RESUMED) with a once-guard), or have ConsentFlowClient/InAppReviewClient accept an explicit Activity for this call path like native did.
verifierNote: Race verified: MainActivity.kt:98/:129 launch on Dispatchers.IO straight from onCreate; the facades resolve the Activity via { ActivityHolder.current } (PlatformModule.android.kt:157-160) and ActivityHolder is set only in onActivityResumed (MyApp.kt:184). AndroidConsentFlowClient.kt:43-46 returns UNKNOWN (and loadAndShowConsentFormIfRequired returns false) when the provider yields null, logged-not-retried for that Activity instance. The IO coroutine has no happens-before with the main-thread create→resume transaction, unlike the Main-dispatched update flow which queues behind it — the KDoc's 'on resume' claim only holds for the latter. Fix (defer to RESUMED or pass the Activity explicitly like native) is behavior-preserving.

title: MyFirebaseMessagingService is exported=true — co-installed apps can start it with crafted MESSAGING_EVENT intents
detail: The FCM service is declared android:exported="true" with the com.google.firebase.MESSAGING_EVENT intent-filter. Firebase's documented manifest template uses exported="false" (Google Play services delivers messages through a privileged path that does not require the service to be exported). Exported=true needlessly lets any co-installed app start the service with the MESSAGING_EVENT action and crafted extras, exercising onMessageReceived's parsing and the notification-posting path (notification spoofing surface: title/body are read straight from data extras with no origin check). Matches native's manifest, but it is a pure hardening regression with a one-word fix and no functional cost.
evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:90-97 `<service android:name=".firebase_cores.messaging.MyFirebaseMessagingService" android:exported="true"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="com.google.firebase.MESSAGING_EVENT" />`.
suggestedFix: Change android:exported to "false" on the MyFirebaseMessagingService declaration (the Firebase-documented value); FCM delivery is unaffected.
